content.text:
Humanity has always been fascinated by the shapes of the things around them. In some early cave paintings, the sun is depicted as a circle. In the cave paintings of Gudahandi in Odisha, one sees numerous geometric patterns including triangles, squares, circles, and ovals. These shapes were likely inspired by what humans saw in nature. Can you recognise the origin of these shapes?
Circles form when raindrops fall on water. The cross-section of a plant stem and the inflorescence of a sunflower are also circular in shape. The full moon and sun also look circular.
What properties are common to all circles, big and small? You have studied one such property in Grade 7. Humans must have noticed it after observing many circular patterns in nature. Every circle has a centre. All points on the circle are at equal distance from the centre. We turn this observation around and make it the definition of a circle.
Activity: List some objects from nature that resemble a circle.

content.text:
1. Look at the pictures: ripples, a stem, a sunflower, the moon, the sun.
2. Every one of them has a centre, and every point of the rim is the same distance from it.
3. This chapter turns that one observation into a definition, then into twelve theorems.
4. Keep a guess in mind: how would you find the centre of a paper circle with no mark on it?
5. And a second guess: when do four points lie on one circle? We settle it at the end.

topics.summary: A circle as a locus: centre, radius, chord, diameter; The circle's symmetries: every turn, every diameter; More to explore: symmetry, chords and loci.

content.text:
When we talk of mathematical shapes such as circles, triangles and squares, we always assume that the figures are drawn on a piece of paper, a two-dimensional plane.
A circle is the set of all points on the plane that are equidistant from a given point on that plane. The set of points that satisfy a given condition is also called the locus of points that satisfy the condition. Using this term, a circle can also be described as the locus of points that are equidistant from a given point. The given point is the centre of the circle. The distance from the centre to any point on the circle is the radius of the circle.
In the figure, A is the centre of the circle. All points on the plane at a distance equal to the length of AB from A form a circle with centre A and radius equal to the length of AB.
Let B and C be two points on the circle. The line segment BC is called a chord of the circle. The angle subtended by the chord BC at the centre is angle BAC. A chord passing through the centre of a circle is called a diameter.

content.text:
1. Fix a point A on the plane and a length AB.
2. Collect every point at distance AB from A: that set is the circle.
3. A set of points fixed by one condition is a locus; the circle is the locus at one distance from A.
4. A is the centre; AB is a radius.
5. B and C on the circle: segment BC is a chord, and ∠BAC is its angle at the centre.
6. A chord through the centre is a diameter.

content.text:
What makes circles so appealing is that they are perfectly symmetrical. Say you are looking at a wheel of a vehicle. You see a point of the wheel touching the ground. When you look at the wheel again after some time, you again see a point of the wheel touching the ground. Can you tell if the two points are the same point? There is no way you can tell; a rotating wheel looks the same at all times! We say the circle has complete rotational symmetry: rotate it by any angle and it looks exactly the same.
Draw a circle on the paper and cut along the circle. Fold the circular paper so that the boundaries overlap, then open it. You see a crease; it is a line of reflection symmetry of the circle. Does this line pass through the centre of the circle? It does. It is a diameter of the circle. All diameters are lines of reflection symmetry.

content.text:
1. A turning wheel looks the same at every instant: turn by any angle, the circle lands on itself.
2. So the circle has complete rotational symmetry about its centre.

content.text:
What are the rotational symmetries of a square? How many lines of reflection symmetry does it have? What about a regular pentagon? A regular hexagon?
Square: turns of 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°, and 4 lines. Regular pentagon: turns of 72° steps (5 in all), 5 lines. Regular hexagon: turns of 60° steps (6 in all), 6 lines. A circle has every turn and every diameter.

The locus of points at a given distance from a given point is a circle. What can we say about the locus of points equidistant from two given points? (Hint: We know that any point that is equidistant from two given points A and B lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Does this make the perpendicular bisector the locus? For this, we have to show that all the points on the perpendicular bisector are equidistant from A and B.)
It is the perpendicular bisector of AB: a point P on it with foot M gives ΔPMA ≅ ΔPMB (SAS), so PA = PB; and every point with PA = PB lies on it.

media.tool_name: Drop some dots. How many circles fit?
media.description: Drop some dots. How many circles fit?. You tap the empty canvas to drop dots, one at a time: A, then B, then C. After one dot you can drag a free centre anywhere; after two, the centre is pinned to a single 'possible centres' line you can slide along; after three, it snaps to one spot and the circle through all three is drawn. Dragging any dot onto the line through the other two collapses both possible-centre lines into two parallel lines that never meet, and no circle is drawn. Starting scene: An empty canvas with one prompt: tap anywhere to drop your first dot. No circle, no lines, no points; the readout strip shows zeros. Open question: Drop some dots on the page. How many circles can pass through all of them? Patterns to look at, one per request, gentle to strong: (1) You have one dot. Drag the centre around, how many circles could pass through just A? (2) Add a second dot. What happened to the place where the centre can live? (3) Look at that line where it crosses AB. (4) Add a third dot and you have two lines. How many points can two lines share? And when can they share none? Break it: Drag any dot onto the line through the other two: with three dots on a line the two possible-centre lines turn parallel, no crossing and no circle is drawn, and the readout shows 'circles: 0'. Dragging the dot back off the line restores the previous state. What stays fixed: Once placed, a dot stays exactly where you leave it; only the centre and the possible-centre lines move as you drag. The tutor: The tutor may ask what you notice as the centre's freedom changes and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never says 'perpendicular bisector', 'circumcentre', 'locus' or 'unique', never states how many circles pass through three points, and never calls an action right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time, from the very first frame; your dots and the collapse you actually watched (region, then line, then point) go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

Case 1: the perpendicular bisector of AB is the line x = 0; the perpendicular bisector of AC is the line x + y = 0, since (x + 4)^2 + (y + 3)^2 = (x - 3)^2 + (y - 4)^2 gives 14x + 14y = 0
Case 1, P high up at (0, 3): PA = PB = sqrt(16 + 36) = sqrt(52), about 7.2; PC = sqrt(9 + 1) = sqrt(10), about 3.2

AB and AC are not parallel because A, B, C are not on one line; lines perpendicular to two non-parallel lines are not parallel, so the two bisectors cross, and two crossing lines share exactly one point

content.text:
Now that we have defined a circle and listed some of its properties, let us ask this question: Given two points A and B on a plane, how many circles pass through A and B?
If a circle passes through A and B, it has a centre, say O. The lengths OA and OB are equal. Is there another point with this property? Yes, the midpoint of segment AB. With the midpoint as centre, a circle passing through A and B can be drawn. Its radius is half the length of AB, and AB is a diameter.
Are there more circles passing through both A and B? Clearly, any point equidistant from A and B can be the centre of a circle passing through A and B. Do you know of such points? We have seen that the perpendicular bisector of the line segment AB is the locus of points equidistant from A and B. Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from A and B, and every point that is equidistant from A and B is on the perpendicular bisector! So, the centres of all circles through A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
In the figure, we see circles through points A and B, and through C and D, and the perpendicular bisector of CD. Every point on the perpendicular bisector is the centre of a circle passing through C and D. So we have circles with centres K, J and L containing points C and D.

You are given two points A and B on a plane. How many squares can you draw on the same plane with A and B on the boundary? How many squares can you draw on the plane with A and B as the corners of the square?
With A and B on the boundary: infinitely many. With A and B as corners: 3, two with AB as a side (one on each side of AB) and one with AB as a diagonal.

content.text:
It is natural to ask: How many circles can you draw through three distinct points A, B and C on a plane? Is there always at least one such circle? Not necessarily! What if A, B and C lie on a straight line, i.e., are collinear? Can you explain why, in this case, there is no circle through A, B and C?
Let us assume that A, B and C are not collinear. Is there always a circle passing through A, B and C? Can there be more than one circle through A, B and C?

content.text:
Why is this true? If there is a circle that passes through non-collinear A, B and C, the circle must have a centre. Let's call that centre O (we will discover O soon).
Since OA = OB, we know that O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Since OA = OC, we know that O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC as well.
But A, B and C are not collinear. So, the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC will intersect at a unique point, since two intersecting lines meet at exactly one point on the plane. That point must be O.
Using O as the centre we can draw a circle with radius equal to the length of OA. That will pass through A, B and C. This explains why the statement is true.
Now three non-collinear points also determine a triangle. What we have described above is the construction of a circle that passes through the vertices of the triangle.
The centre O of the circle that passes through the vertices A, B and C of ΔABC is called the circumcentre of ΔABC. The circle is called the circumcircle and is said to circumscribe the triangle. Conversely, the triangle is said to be inscribed in the circle. Since, the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC is a single point, there is just one such circle for a given triangle. Further, for an acute-angled triangle, the circumcentre lies inside the triangle. For an obtuse-angled triangle, the circumcentre lies outside the triangle. And for a right-angled triangle, the circumcentre lies at the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

content.text:
Theorem 1: There is a unique circle passing through three non-collinear points.
Given: A, B and C are three points that are not collinear.
To show: Exactly one circle passes through A, B and C.
1. Suppose a circle passes through A, B and C; call its centre O.
2. OA = OB, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
3. OA = OC, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC.
4. A, B and C are not collinear, so these two bisectors are not parallel.
5. Two intersecting lines meet at exactly one point, so O is that one point.
6. With centre O and radius OA, the circle passes through A, B and C.
7. There is only one choice of O, so the circle is unique.

maths_rules: AB = 5 cm, angle A = 70 degrees, angle B = 60 degrees
angle C = 180 - 70 - 60 = 50 degrees
By the sine rule, 2R = AB / sin C = 5 / sin 50 = 5 / 0.7660 = 6.527, so R = 3.26 cm (about 3.3 cm); OA = OB = OC = 3.26 cm
BC = 2R sin A = 6.527 x 0.9397 = 6.13 cm; AC = 2R sin B = 6.527 x 0.8660 = 5.65 cm; the figure is drawn to these lengths
70, 60 and 50 are all less than 90, so the triangle is acute-angled and O lies inside it
the slip's point is where the angle halvers meet (the incentre I). Area = 0.5 x 5 x 5.65 x sin 70 = 13.28; half the perimeter = (5 + 6.13 + 5.65) / 2 = 8.39; inradius r = 13.28 / 8.39 = 1.58 cm
IA = r / sin 35 = 2.76 cm, IB = r / sin 30 = 3.16 cm, IC = r / sin 25 = 3.74 cm; the circle from I through A (radius 2.76) falls short of B and C
The circumcircle is drawn with centre O and radius 3.26 cm through A, B and C

maths_rules: AB = 6 cm, BC = 7 cm, CA = 7 cm; the triangle has two equal sides, CA = CB
M is the midpoint of AB, AM = MB = 3 cm; CM is the height from C, square to AB
O lies on CM because CA = CB; with R = OA = OC: R^2 = 3^2 + (CM - R)^2, so 2 x CM x R = 9 + 40 = 49, and R = 49 / (2 x 6.325) = 3.87 cm, about 3.9 cm; exactly 49 sqrt(10) / 40 cm
OM = CM - R = 6.32 - 3.87 = 2.45 cm, so O is about 2.5 cm above AB, inside the triangle
Check: OA = sqrt(3^2 + 2.45^2) = sqrt(9 + 6.01) = sqrt(15.01) = 3.87 cm, equal to OC
Angle C: cos C = (49 + 49 - 36) / (2 x 7 x 7) = 62 / 98, so angle C = 50.7 degrees; angles A and B = 64.6 degrees each; all are less than 90
the slip's point is halfway up CM: its distance to C = CM / 2 = sqrt(10) = 3.16 cm (about 3.2); its distance to A = sqrt(9 + 10) = sqrt(19) = 4.36 cm (about 4.4)

video_script.anchor: What is the least radius of a circle through A and B?
video_script.design: One idea: AB is a chord of every such circle, and the diameter is the longest chord. Assumes: the centres lie on the perpendicular bisector; chord and diameter. Wrong idea: The slip thinks the circle can shrink to nothing. The anchor stays all video; one hard clear before the idea.
never_show: a radius smaller than half of AB
video_script.wrong_move: The slip thinks sliding the centre closer keeps shrinking the circle to nothing; the circle must still reach A and B, so it can never be narrower than AB
maths_rules: A and B are two fixed points; every circle through both has its centre P on the perpendicular bisector of AB
The radius of the circle with centre P is PA (= PB)
M is the midpoint of AB; for P on the bisector, PM is square to AB, so PA^2 = PM^2 + MA^2, which is at least MA^2; PA is smallest when P = M
AB is a chord of every circle through A and B; no chord is longer than a diameter, so 2 x radius is at least AB, and the radius is at least AB / 2
When P = M, AB is a diameter and the radius is AB / 2; this is the least radius
Example on screen: AB = 8 cm, MA = 4 cm; P at 3 cm from M gives PA = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 cm; P at M gives PA = 4 cm = half of 8 cm
the slip's shrink-to-nothing idea fails: any circle through A and B contains the chord AB of length 8 cm, so its diameter is at least 8 cm
video_script.payoff_line: The least radius is half the length of eigh B

final_answer.spoken: half the length of eigh B

video_script.substitution: AB is a chord of every such circle, and a chord is never longer than a diameter.
video_script.wrong_answer: the circle shrinks to nothing

content.text:
Circles Through Given Points, Q1: Draw ΔABC with AB = 5 cm, ∠A = 70° and ∠B = 60°. Draw the circumcircle of ΔABC. Is the centre inside or outside the triangle?
1. Draw AB = 5 cm; at A draw 70° and at B draw 60°; the rays meet at C.
2. ∠C = 180° − 70° − 60° = 50°.
3. Draw the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC; they meet at O.
4. With centre O and radius OA, draw the circle through A, B and C.
5. All three angles (70°, 60°, 50°) are acute, so the triangle is acute-angled.
Answer: The centre O is inside the triangle, because every angle of ΔABC is acute.

Draw the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC; they meet at O.
With centre O and radius OA, draw the circle through A, B and C.
All three angles (70°, 60°, 50°) are acute, so the triangle is acute-angled.

Circles Through Given Points, Q2: Draw ΔABC with AB = 5 cm, ∠A = 100°, AC = 4 cm. Draw the circumcircle of ΔABC. Is the centre inside or outside the triangle?
1. Draw AB = 5 cm; at A draw 100°; mark C on that ray with AC = 4 cm; join BC.
2. Draw the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC; they meet at O.
3. With centre O and radius OA, draw the circle through A, B and C.
4. ∠A = 100° is obtuse, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.
Answer: The centre O is outside the triangle, beyond the longest side BC, because ∠A is obtuse.

Circles Through Given Points, Q3: Draw ΔABC, with AB = 6 cm, BC = 7 cm and CA = 7 cm. Draw the circumcircle of ΔABC. Let the circumcentre be O. Measure OA, OB, OC.
1. Draw AB = 6 cm; arcs of 7 cm from A and from B meet at C.
2. Draw the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC; they meet at O.
3. OA, OB and OC are all radii of the circumcircle, so they measure the same.
4. CA = CB = 7 cm, so O lies on the altitude from C; its foot M is the midpoint of AB, with AM = 3 cm.
5. CM = √(7² − 3²) = √40 cm, about 6.32 cm.
6. With R = OA = OC: R² = 3² + (CM − R)², so 2 × CM × R = 49, and R = 49 ÷ (2√40) ≈ 3.87 cm.
Answer: OA = OB = OC, each about 3.9 cm (exactly 49√10/40 cm).

content.text:
Circles Through Given Points, Q4: What is the least possible radius of a circle through two points A and B?
1. Every circle through A and B has AB as a chord.
2. No chord is longer than a diameter, so the diameter is at least AB.
3. The circle with centre at the midpoint of AB has AB as its diameter.
Answer: Half the length of AB, for the circle with centre at the midpoint of AB.

content.text:
Draw and Decide, Q1: A, B and C are three collinear points. Can you find a point P such that PA = PB = PC? What can you say about the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC? Draw and check. Can you show that for three collinear points A, B and C, the perpendicular bisector of AB and BC are parallel? Is it possible for a circle to pass through collinear points? Can you draw a line that cuts a given circle in three distinct points?
1. PA = PB puts P on the perpendicular bisector of AB; PB = PC puts P on the perpendicular bisector of BC.
2. Both bisectors are perpendicular to the same line ABC, so they are parallel.
3. They are different lines, since the midpoints of AB and BC are different points.
4. Parallel lines never meet, so no point P exists.
5. So no circle passes through three collinear points, and no line cuts a circle in three points.
Answer: No such P exists; the two bisectors are parallel; no circle passes through three collinear points; a line meets a circle in at most two points.

content.text:
Draw and Decide, Q2: The circumcircle of a given ΔABC is drawn. Can there be other triangles congruent to ΔABC that share the same circumcircle?
1. Rotate ΔABC about the centre O by any angle: the vertices stay on the circle.
2. A rotation keeps every length, so the new triangle is congruent to ΔABC.
3. Reflecting in any diameter also keeps the circle and the lengths.
Answer: Yes, infinitely many: every rotation of ΔABC about the centre, and every reflection in a diameter.

media.title: Spin the wheel: what does the centre see?
media.context: Class 9 'I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round' (circles). The idea playground for Th2, Th3: it opens when the student first meets the statement, before the proof and its explanation video. It never walks the student through a proof: a live figure, a small kit, a notebook for the student's own guesses, a Break it panel, and patterns to look at, offered only on request or when the student seems stuck. The explanation follows whether or not the student finds a reason. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.tool_name: Spin the wheel: what does the centre see?
media.description: Spin the wheel: what does the centre see?. You drag a chord all the way round a circle: dragging its body or either endpoint rotates it, its length stays fixed, and the angle it makes at the centre C refuses to change. A length stepper changes the chord's length instead, and each distinct value logs a row in a table. You can add a second chord with its own stepper, and when the two lengths match, their angles at C match too. Once you ask for it, the two radii to each chord's ends are drawn; once you ask again, you can lock the angle at C and try, and fail, to change the chord's length. Starting scene: One circle, centre C marked, one chord at a seeded angle with length equal to the radius. No radii are drawn. The readout strip shows the chord's length and its angle at C. Open question: A thread is tied across a wheel. Spin the wheel. What does the centre see? Patterns to look at, one per request, gentle to strong: (1) Take the thread all the way round the wheel. What changed? (2) Now make the thread longer. What moved with it? (3) Join both ends of the thread to the centre. What shape do you see? (4) Two of the three sides are always the radius. So what decides the triangle's shape? (5) Lock the angle at the centre. Now try to change the chord. Break it: Lock the angle at the centre (rung 5): the chord still rotates freely, but the length stepper springs back every time you try to change it, refusing the resize. That refusal is the discovery, matching chords cannot match angles and then let one length slip away. What stays fixed: The circle and its centre C stay fixed; a chord's length only changes through its stepper, never by dragging. The tutor: The tutor may ask what stayed the same as you spun the wheel and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never says 'subtend', 'congruent', 'SSS', 'SAS' or 'isosceles', never states the result, and never says right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time; your table of lengths and angles, and whether you matched two chords and felt the lock, go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

phases.A_rotate: Drag the chord right around; len and angle at C sit still, the angle arc sweeps with the chord keeping its size. Coach after a full turn: 'You've taken it all the way round. What changed?' Fires rotation_changes_nothing after >= 300 degrees cumulative rotation. Build thin, ~40s of work.
phases.B_resize: Stepper changes len; the angle moves with it; each distinct value logs a table row. Landmark at len=5.0 tags 'chord = radius' at exactly 60 degrees (Exercise 5.6 Q1, p.19); at len=10.0 tags 'longest chord' (Think & Reflect Q2, p.3).
phases.C_two_chords: Add a second chord, each with its own stepper, rotating independently. When |len1-len2| < 0.05, both angle readouts match and the two arcs draw in the same colour with matching tick counts. Fires equal_len_equal_angle.
phases.D_radii_reveal: Rung 3: draw CA, CB (and CD, CE). Two triangles appear, all four radii tick-marked the same. Coach: 'Two of the three sides are always the radius.' The moment the picture stops being a chord and becomes a triangle.
phases.E_locked_angle: Rung 5, the only part distinguishing Theorem 2 from Theorem 3. Toggle 'Lock the angle at C': theta still rotates freely, but the length stepper is refused (120ms +-3u shake, cue bad, refusals++), coach 'The angle is fixed. Can you make the chord any other length?' Fires angle_fixes_length on the second refusal. Do not cut this phase; a static diagram cannot distinguish implication direction, but a constraint you push against and lose to can.

maths_rules: Angle at the centre made by a chord of length c in a circle of radius r: 2 x arcsin(c / (2r)); readings are to the nearest degree
Circle of radius 4 cm. Chord 4 cm: 2 x arcsin(4/8) = 2 x 30° = 60° exactly (triangle with three sides of 4 cm). Both chords of 4 cm read 60°

CA = CD because both are radii; CB = CE because both are radii; AB = DE given

media.tool_name: Slide the point. Can you light just one lamp?
media.description: Slide the point. Can you light just one lamp?. You slide a point M along a chord AB and watch two lamps: one for 'equal halves' (AM = MB) and one for 'right angle' (the segment from the centre meets the chord at 90 degrees). The two lamps light together only at one spot, the foot, and never separately, however hard you try. You can also drag the chord's ends to try a new chord, and, once you ask for it, move the line's starting point off the centre to see the two lamps come apart. Starting scene: A circle, centre C, one chord AB at a seeded position, and a point M on the chord deliberately off the midpoint. The segment CM is drawn. Both lamps are off. Open question: Slide the point along the thread. Can you light just one lamp? Patterns to look at, one per request, gentle to strong: (1) Slide the point along the chord. Watch the two halves. (2) Now watch the angle at the same time. (3) Try to light just one lamp. (4) Join the centre to both ends of the chord. Two triangles, what is the same in each? (5) The two angles at the point are equal, and they sit on a straight line. So how big is each? Break it: Move the line's start off the centre (rung 3): the length lamp still lights at the midpoint, but the angle lamp now lights somewhere else entirely, and the two lamps come apart. That is why the theorem says 'from the centre'. What stays fixed: The circle and its centre C stay fixed; M always stays on the chord, between A and B. The tutor: The tutor may ask which lamp lit first (neither, that's the point) and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never says 'perpendicular bisector', 'congruent', 'bisects' or 'linear pair', never says the two conditions are equivalent, and never says right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time; how many chords you tried, how many times you failed to light just one lamp, and whether you moved the line off the centre, go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

maths_rules: Circle of radius 4 cm, centre C at (0, 0)

Chord 1: A (-3.2, -2.4), B (3.2, -2.4); both on the circle since 3.2 x 3.2 + 2.4 x 2.4 = 10.24 + 5.76 = 16; length 6.4 cm; midpoint M (0, -2.4); AM = MB = 3.2 cm; CM is vertical and AB horizontal, so the angle at M reads 90°
Chord 2: a chord 3.2 cm from C; half chord = square root of (16 - 10.24) = square root of 5.76 = 2.4 cm; length 4.8 cm; AM = MB = 2.4 cm; the angle at its midpoint reads 90°

The slip's case on chord 1: M at (1.2, -2.4), 1.2 cm right of the midpoint; AM = 4.4 cm, MB = 2.0 cm; MC = (-1.2, 2.4); angle CMA = arctan(2.4 / 1.2) = 63.43°, shown as 63°; angle CMB = 180° - 63.43° = 116.57°, shown as 117°
Given: circle with centre C, chord AB, M the midpoint of AB. To prove: CM ⊥ AB. Construction: join CA and CB
CA = CB because both are radii, so ∆CAB is isosceles and ∠CAM = ∠CBM (angles facing the equal sides)
AM = BM because M is the midpoint
SAS: CA = CB, ∠CAM = ∠CBM (between CA and AM, and between CB and BM), AM = BM, so ∆CMA ≅ ∆CMB, giving ∠CMA = ∠CMB
∠CMA + ∠CMB = 180° (angles on a straight line); two equal angles adding to 180° are 90° each, so CM ⊥ AB
Question for the child: can the line from the centre to a chord's midpoint meet the chord at 80°? No, by the theorem; the answer is never shown

content.text:
You may want to know when 4 points lie on the same circle. That will have to wait till the end of this chapter. We need to do some more work to get there.
Tie a thread at two points on a wheel; pull it tight. The thread can be thought of as a chord of the wheel (a circle). Imagine joining the end points of the thread to the centre. The thread subtends an angle at the centre. Now, rotate the wheel. The thread rotates around the centre along with the wheel.
In the new position, the thread is another chord on the circle. What is common to the first and second chords? They have the same length, equal to the length of the thread. What about the angle subtended by the second chord at the centre? It must surely be the same as the angle subtended by the first chord at the centre. We now explain why this is true.

content.text:
What does the theorem say? It talks of two chords of the circle with equal length. In geometry, it always helps to draw a figure! AB and DE are chords of the same length. We need to explain why ∠ACB is equal to ∠DCE. What are we given? AB = DE.
To explain why two angles in two different triangles are equal, we use congruence of triangles. If the angles which we want to show equal are corresponding angles, then our task would be done!
Given: AB = DE. To show: ∠ACB = ∠DCE.
Why is this true? First, we see that CA = CB = r, the radius of the circle. Also, CD = CE = r. So, CA = CD and CB = CE. But AB = DE is given! By the SSS congruence, ∆CAB is congruent to ∆CDE. So, ∠ACB is equal to ∠DCE, i.e., the angles subtended at the centre are equal.

content.text:
Theorem 2: Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre of the circle.
Given: AB = DE, chords of a circle with centre C.
To show: ∠ACB = ∠DCE.
1. CA = CB = r and CD = CE = r (radii).
2. So CA = CD and CB = CE.
3. AB = DE (given).
4. By SSS, ∆CAB ≅ ∆CDE.
5. Corresponding angles are equal, so ∠ACB = ∠DCE.

content.text:
Now suppose we have two chords that subtend equal angles at the centre. Are the chords equal? What does our intuition tell us? Let the chords be AB and DE. Let us use our imagination. Assume that B, A, E, and D are located clockwise on the circle as shown in the figure, where a = 54° and b = 54°.
Imagine you are standing at the centre C of a circle. Stretch your arms so that they are at a certain angle. Let your arms intersect the circle at A, B. The distance between your arm ends must be the length of chord AB. Now let the floor rotate magically. You start rotating (say clockwise) about C. Don't change the angle your arms make! At some point your left arm meets point E.
Where will your right hand be? It should be at D, should it not? That is because we assumed that angles ACB and DCF are equal, and you have not moved your hands. The distance between the ends of your arms must be the length of DE as well. Let us now explain why this is true.
Let us draw the figure. Given: ∠ACB = ∠DCE. To show: AB = ED.
Why is this true? We see that AC = BC = the radius of the circle. Likewise, EC = DC = the radius. So, AC = DC and BC = EC. Since, ∠ACB = ∠DCE, by the SAS congruence, ∆ACB ≅ ∆DCE. Hence, AB = ED.

content.text:
Theorem 3: Chords of a circle that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal.
Given: ∠ACB = ∠DCE, where C is the centre.
To show: AB = ED.
1. AC = BC = r and EC = DC = r (radii).
2. So AC = DC and BC = EC.
3. ∠ACB = ∠DCE (given).
4. By SAS, ∆ACB ≅ ∆DCE.
5. Corresponding sides are equal, so AB = ED.

content.text:
Let us see why this is true. Draw a circle with centre C. Draw any chord AB. Let M be the midpoint of AB. We must show that CM is perpendicular to AB.
Explanation: CAB is an isosceles triangle. AB is the base and CA = CB. So, ∠A = ∠B. M is the midpoint of AB. So, AM = BM. By the SAS congruence, ∆CMA is congruent to ∆CMB. So, ∠CMB = ∠CMA. But ∠CMB + ∠CMA = 180° (angles on a line). So, both angles are 90°. That is, CM is perpendicular to AB.

content.text:
Theorem 4: The line joining the centre of a circle and the midpoint of a chord of the circle is perpendicular to the chord.
Given: A circle with centre C, a chord AB and its midpoint M.
To show: CM is perpendicular to AB.
1. CA = CB (radii), so ∆CAB is isosceles and ∠A = ∠B.
2. AM = BM, because M is the midpoint of AB.
3. By SAS, ∆CMA ≅ ∆CMB.
4. So ∠CMB = ∠CMA.
5. ∠CMB + ∠CMA = 180° (angles on a line).
6. So each angle is 90°, and CM is perpendicular to AB.

video_script.design: One idea: both sides from the centre are radii. Assumes: all radii are equal, and the meaning of isosceles. Slip: The slip takes the chord for a radius. The anchor question stays all video; the circle stays from ground to idea; one hard clear before the recap.

maths_rules: O is the centre, A and B are points of the circle, AB is a chord that does not pass through O (if it did, O, A and B would lie on one line and there would be no triangle)
OA is a radius because it joins the centre to a point of the circle; OB is a radius for the same reason; all radii of one circle are equal, so OA = OB = r
A triangle with two equal sides is isosceles, so ΔOAB is isosceles
the slip's case: circle of radius 4 cm with a chord of 7 cm; OA = 4 cm but AB = 7 cm, so the chord is not a radius; a chord is at most the diameter, 8 cm here
Check: every chord not through the centre gives the same two radii as sides, whatever its length

video_script.anchor: Triangle ABC sits in a circle with AB = AC. Does the altitude from A pass through the centre?
video_script.design: One idea: the altitude is the perpendicular bisector, and the centre must be on it. Assumes: RHS, and the perpendicular bisector fact. Slip: The slip drops the equal sides. The anchor stays all video; the circle stays from ground to idea; one hard clear before the recap.

maths_rules: Circle of radius 4 cm, centre O at (0, 0). B (-3.2, -2.4) and C (3.2, -2.4) are on the circle (10.24 + 5.76 = 16); BC = 6.4 cm
Isosceles case: A (0, 4); AB = AC = square root of (3.2 x 3.2 + 6.4 x 6.4) = square root of 51.2 = 7.16 cm; the altitude from A is the line x = 0, meeting BC at D (0, -2.4), and it passes through O

the slip's case: A' (-2.4, 3.2) on the circle (5.76 + 10.24 = 16); A'B = square root of (0.64 + 31.36) = square root of 32 = 5.66 cm, A'C = square root of (31.36 + 31.36) = square root of 62.72 = 7.92 cm; the altitude from A' is the line x = -2.4, which misses O by 2.4 cm
Proof: D is the foot of the altitude from A, so ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°; AB = AC (given); AD is common; RHS gives ΔADB ≅ ΔADC, so BD = DC
AD meets BC at its midpoint at a right angle, so AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC
OB = OC because both are radii; every point the same distance from B and C lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC; so O lies on AD

maths_rules: Circle radius 5 cm, centre O. Chord 1 is 6 cm, chord 2 is 8 cm, parallel, on opposite sides of O

The perpendicular from O to each chord meets it at its midpoint (a square line from the centre halves a chord); both perpendiculars lie on one line through O, square to both parallel chords; call the midpoints M (6 cm chord) and N (8 cm chord)
Half chords: 6 / 2 = 3 cm and 8 / 2 = 4 cm
OM: 5 x 5 = 25, 3 x 3 = 9, 25 - 9 = 16, square root of 16 = 4, so OM = 4 cm
ON: 25 - 4 x 4 = 25 - 16 = 9, square root of 9 = 3, so ON = 3 cm
Opposite sides of O, so MN = OM + ON = 4 + 3 = 7 cm
the slip: 5 - 3 = 2; check 2 x 2 + 3 x 3 = 4 + 9 = 13, not 25, so 2 is not the distance
Checks: 3 x 3 + 4 x 4 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5 x 5; each distance is less than the radius 5; MN = 7 is less than the diameter 10; on the same side the distances would be taken away instead

Chords and the Centre, Q1: Show that the triangle formed by a chord and the centre of the circle is isosceles.

The Perpendicular from the Centre, Q1: Can you explain why the converse to Theorem 4 is true, i.e., why does the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord of the circle bisect the chord?
Hint: Use the figure. You are told that ∠CMA = ∠CMB = 90°. You need to show that AM = BM.

content.text:
Chords and the Centre, Q2: Show that if two such isosceles triangles (occurring in the previous question) have equal base length, they are congruent to each other.
1. Take chords AB and DE of the same circle with centre O, and AB = DE.
2. OA = OD and OB = OE (all radii).
3. AB = DE (given).
4. By SSS, ΔOAB ≅ ΔODE.
Answer: The two triangles are congruent by SSS.

content.text:
The Perpendicular from the Centre, Q2: An isosceles triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle, with AB = AC. Show that the altitude from A to BC passes through the centre of the circle.
1. Let D be the foot of the altitude from A, so AD ⊥ BC.
2. AB = AC and AD is common, and both angles at D are 90°, so ΔADB ≅ ΔADC (RHS) and BD = DC.
3. So AD is the perpendicular bisector of the chord BC.
4. The centre O is equidistant from B and C, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC.
Answer: The altitude from A is the perpendicular bisector of chord BC, and the centre lies on it.

So AD is the perpendicular bisector of the chord BC.
The centre O is equidistant from B and C, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC.

content.text:
The Perpendicular from the Centre, Q3: Two parallel chords of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm are on opposite sides of the centre of a circle. If the radius of the circle is 5 cm, find the distance between the midpoints of the chords.
1. The perpendicular from the centre bisects each chord; half chords are 3 cm and 4 cm.
2. Distance of the 6 cm chord: √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 cm.
3. Distance of the 8 cm chord: √(5² − 4²) = √9 = 3 cm.
4. The chords are on opposite sides of the centre, so add: 4 + 3 = 7 cm.
Answer: 7 cm.
steps: The perpendicular from the centre bisects each chord; half chords are 3 cm and 4 cm.
Distance of the 6 cm chord: √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 cm.
Distance of the 8 cm chord: √(5² − 4²) = √9 = 3 cm.
The chords are on opposite sides of the centre, so add: 4 + 3 = 7 cm.
content.answer: 7 cm.

media.tool_name: How far is each chord from the centre?
media.description: How far is each chord from the centre?. You drag two chords AB and FG round a circle with centre C and see the perpendiculars CE and CH. You can lock the two lengths or the two distances together, draw radii, mark what you know, write guesses, try to break them, and switch off a condition. Starting scene: AB and FG have the same length and point in very different directions. The two perpendiculars from C are drawn; no radii are. Open question: Two chords have the same length. Are they the same distance from the centre, or can one be closer? And the other way round? Patterns to look at, one per request, gentle to strong: (1) Look at the lines from C to all four chord ends. (2) Look at the half chord, the distance line and the radius at one end. What shape do they make? (3) Look at the two right triangles, one on each chord, side by side. (4) Compare those two triangles part by part: the right angle, the longest side, and one more side. Break it: Switch off 'same circle' and equal chords in circles of different sizes sit at different distances; switch off 'measured square to the chord' and a slanted distance from C stops matching. What stays fixed: The circle and its centre C stay fixed; each perpendicular stays square to its chord. The tutor: The tutor may ask what you notice, ask which marks you measured and which you know, and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never states the result, never names the congruence, and never says right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time; your notebook and figure go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

video_script.anchor: Are equal chords of one circle always the same distance from its centre?
video_script.design: One idea: equal radii make copies, so equal chords sit at equal distances. Assumes: S S S and R H S, and that the line from the centre to a chord's midpoint is square to it. Wrong idea: the slip drops 'one circle'. The anchor stays all video; the proof figure arrives at the idea part and stays to the end. Two hard clears: the circles leave at the idea part, the figure shrinks at the recap.
never_show: a forty centimetre chord at fifteen centimetres in the bigger circle
a slanted line labelled as the distance
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip says a forty centimetre chord sits fifteen centimetres from the centre on any circle; in a bigger circle of radius twenty-nine it sits twenty-one away, so the claim needs both chords in one circle.
video_script.callback_to: the explore tool 'How far is each chord from the centre?' on M3.S5.T5.C18
maths_rules: circle 1: a circle of radius 25 cm with centre C
a chord of length 40 cm in it has half chord 20 cm; its distance from C is √(25² − 20²) = √(625 − 400) = √225 = 15 cm
a chord of length 30 cm has half chord 15 cm; its distance is √(625 − 225) = √400 = 20 cm
case 1: two 40 cm chords in different places and directions, each drawn 15 cm from C; case 2: two 30 cm chords, each drawn 20 cm from C
the distance of a chord from the centre is the length of the line from C that meets the chord at a right angle; every other line from C to the chord is longer
circle 2 (the slip's break): a circle of radius 29 cm; a 40 cm chord there has distance √(29² − 20²) = √(841 − 400) = √441 = 21 cm, not 15 cm

proof figure: circle with centre C; chords AB and FG with AB = FG; E and H are the midpoints of AB and FG; because the line from the centre to a midpoint is square to the chord, CE ⊥ AB and CH ⊥ FG, so CE and CH are the distances
way 1: CA = CF (radii), CB = CG (radii), AB = FG (given); SSS gives ΔCAB ≅ ΔCFG; congruent triangles have equal heights on matching bases, so CE = CH
way 2: AE = FH (halves of equal chords, E and H are midpoints); ∠CEA = ∠CHF = 90°; CA = CF (radii, the longest sides); RHS gives ΔCEA ≅ ΔCHF, so CE = CH
recap question: in two circles of different sizes, the step CA = CF fails, because the radii are no longer equal
video_script.payoff_line: Equal chords of one circle are the same distance from its centre

final_answer.spoken: C E equals C H

video_script.substitution: All four lines from the centre to the chord ends are radii, so the two triangles are exact copies and their heights from the centre match.

media.tool_name: Long chord, short chord: where do they sit?
media.description: Long chord, short chord: where do they sit?. You drag two chords AB and DE nearer to and further from the centre C, pin their lengths and distances, and record rows in a small table. You can show squares on the sides of a triangle, write guesses, try to break them, and put a chord in a different circle. Starting scene: AB is long and DE is short, placed on opposite sides of C. The table is empty. Open question: One chord is longer than another. Which one sits closer to the centre, or does it depend? Patterns to look at, one per request, gentle to strong: (1) Look at the right triangle made by a radius, the distance line and half the chord. (2) Drag the chord and watch that triangle. Which side never changes length? (3) Show the squares on the three sides of that triangle and watch their areas as the chord moves. (4) Look at a right triangle whose longest side is fixed, and at its other two sides together. Break it: Switch off 'same circle' and put the shorter chord in a smaller circle: it can then sit nearer its own centre than the longer chord sits to its centre. What stays fixed: The circle, and so its radius, stays fixed while the chords move. The tutor: The tutor may ask what the table shows, ask what stays the same in the triangle, and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never states the result, never writes the squares out as a step, and never says right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time; your table, notebook and figure go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

media.description: A table of chord lengths and distances in a circle of radius twenty-five centimetres shows that longer chords sit nearer the centre. A chord in a smaller circle seems to break the rule until we see the rule is about one circle. The video states the theorem; the proof then uses the Baudhayana Pythagoras theorem: both triangles add up to the same radius squared, so the bigger half chord leaves the smaller distance.

video_script.why: The table showed the longer chord nearer the centre in every row; why must that happen in every circle?

content.text:
Activity: Take a paper circle. Fold the circle from the boundary, inwards. Open the fold. The crease is now a chord. Now fold the paper again, so that the end points of the chord meet. Open the fold.
Measure the lengths of the parts into which the chord is divided. The chord gets bisected where the folds intersect. Measure the angle between the creases. The crease of the second fold is along the perpendicular from the centre to the chord. Measure the distance from the centre to the midpoint of the chord. It is the distance from the centre to the chord.
Now draw another chord of the same length. How will you do this? We will let you figure this out yourself. Join the centre to the midpoint of the new chord and measure its length. Is it the same as distance from the centre to the first chord?
Now take a tracing paper and draw a circle on it with the same radius. Place the circle on the tracing paper on top of the circle paper so that the circles overlap. Trace the chord on the circle paper, and the perpendicular to it from its centre, onto the tracing paper circle. Now rotate the tracing paper. You will see the chord through the tracing paper, it looks like a different chord of the same length on the circle paper.
The circle is a symmetric figure. So, rotating the circle around its centre does not change the circle. As we rotate the circle, our chosen chord will also rotate, to give a new chord of the same length. Along with it, the perpendicular from the centre to the chord also moves! Equal chords appear to be equidistant from the centre.
Is this a totally convincing explanation? No, we have only given examples where our guess holds true. A statement may be true on a large number of examples, but it does not mean the statement is true in general. So let us explain why the statement is true.

Draw the figure. Given: Circle with centre C; AB = FG; E, H are midpoints of AB, FG respectively. To show: CE = CH.
Why is this true? From Theorem 5, CE and CH are the perpendiculars from C to the chords AB and FG respectively. So, CE and CH are the distances from the centre C to the chords AB and FG respectively. We shall explain this result in two different ways.
(1) Triangles CAB and CFG are congruent. CA = CF (both are equal to the radius of the circle). Likewise, CB = CG. We are given that AB = FG. So, by the SSS congruence, ∆CAB ≅ ∆CFG. Hence the altitudes of the congruent triangles are congruent. CE = CH. Therefore, the chords AB and FG are equidistant from the centre C.
(2) Consider triangles CEA and CHF. From Theorem 5, the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. Hence, E and H are the midpoints of the chords AB and FG respectively. AE = FH (since AB = FG, and E and H are midpoints of AB and FG). ∠CEA = ∠CHF = 90°. CF = CA, as they are radii of the circle. By the RHS congruence, ∆CEA ≅ ∆CHF. So, CE = CH. Thus the chords of equal length are equidistant from the centre.

Theorem 6: Chords of a circle having the same length are all at the same distance from the centre of the circle.
Given: Circle with centre C; AB = FG; E, H are midpoints of AB, FG.
To show: CE = CH.
1. By Theorem 5, CE and CH are the perpendiculars from C to AB and FG.
2. Way 1: CA = CF and CB = CG (radii), and AB = FG (given).
3. By SSS, ∆CAB ≅ ∆CFG, so their altitudes CE and CH are equal.
4. Way 2: AE = FH, since AB = FG and E, H are midpoints.
5. ∠CEA = ∠CHF = 90° and CA = CF (radii).
6. By RHS, ∆CEA ≅ ∆CHF, so CE = CH.

Which of the two unequal chords is farther from the centre? You have two chords on a circle. One is longer than the other. Which chord is closer to the centre? Can you guess?

content.text:
As always, we draw the figure. Remember: by 'distance from C to AB' we mean the perpendicular distance. So, we drop perpendiculars CF and CG from C to AB and DE, respectively. Given: AB > DE. To show that: CF < CG.
Why is this true? In the figure, both AC and CD are radii. So, AC = CD. By the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem, CD² = CG² + GD² and AC² = CF² + AF². So, CF² + AF² = CG² + GD². Now AB is greater than DE. So AF is greater than GD (because F and G are the midpoints of AB and DE). Since AF² > GD² we have CF² < CG². So, CF < CG.
Comment: The chord nearest to the centre is the chord containing the centre. Its distance to C is zero! So the diameter is the greatest chord. If one pushes the chord away from the centre, at some stage the chord becomes a single point, its length is zero, and the distance of C from this chord is the radius.

content.text:
Theorem 8: Let AB and DE be two chords of a circle with centre C. Suppose AB > DE. Then the distance from C to AB is less than the distance from C to DE.
Given: AB > DE; CF ⊥ AB and CG ⊥ DE.
To show: CF < CG.
1. AC = CD (radii).
2. By the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem, AC² = CF² + AF² and CD² = CG² + GD².
3. So CF² + AF² = CG² + GD².
4. F and G are the midpoints of AB and DE, and AB > DE, so AF > GD.
5. So AF² > GD², which forces CF² < CG².
6. So CF < CG: the longer chord is nearer the centre.

video_script.design: One idea: R H S on the half-chord triangles, then double the halves. Assumes: R H S, that the square-on line from the centre halves a chord, and that distance means the square-on line. Wrong idea: the slip measures along a slanted line. maths_rules: the figure is a circle of radius 50 cm with centre C
a chord 30 cm from C: half chord = √(50² − 30²) = √(2500 − 900) = √1600 = 40 cm, so the chord is 80 cm
a chord 14 cm from C: half chord = √(2500 − 196) = √2304 = 48 cm, so the chord is 96 cm
case 1: two chords in different places, each 30 cm from C, each 80 cm long; case 2: two chords, each 14 cm from C, each 96 cm long

the slip's break: a slanted line of 30 cm from C to a point of the 96 cm chord (that point is √(900 − 196) = √704, about 26.5 cm, from the chord's foot, inside the half chord of 48 cm); the square-on distance of that chord is 14 cm
proof figure: circle with centre C; chords AB and FG; E on AB and H on FG with CE ⊥ AB, CH ⊥ FG and CE = CH
construction: join CA and CF
CA = CF (radii, each the longest side, facing a right angle); CE = CH (given); ∠CEA = ∠CHF = 90°; RHS gives ΔCEA ≅ ΔCHF, so AE = FH (matching sides)
the square-on line from the centre halves the chord, so E and H are the midpoints: AB = 2AE and FG = 2FH, so AB = FG
closing question: two chords of one circle with different lengths cannot sit at the same distance, because the theorem would force them to be equal; its answer is not shown
video_script.payoff_line: Chords of one circle at the same distance from its centre have equal length

final_answer.spoken: eigh B equals F G

Chords at Equal Distance, Q1: Use the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem to show why Theorem 6 must be true.
1. In ΔCEA, CE² = CA² − AE².
2. In ΔCHF, CH² = CF² − FH².
3. CA = CF = r, and AE = FH because the equal chords are bisected.
4. So CE² = CH², and CE = CH.
Answer: CE² = r² − AE² = r² − FH² = CH², so CE = CH.

Chords at Equal Distance, Q2: Consider the figure. If CE is perpendicular to AB, CH is perpendicular to GH, and CE = CH, show that AB = GF.
1. CA = CF (radii) and CE = CH (given).

3. By RHS, ΔCEA ≅ ΔCHF, so AE = FH.
4. The perpendicular from the centre bisects each chord, so AB = 2AE and FG = 2FH.
5. So AB = GF.
Answer: AB = GF: by RHS the half chords are equal. This is Theorem 7.

content.text:
Chord Length and Distance, Q2: Explain why the following statement is true: If the perpendicular distance of a chord from the centre is d and the radius is r, then the chord length is 2√(r² − d²).
1. The perpendicular from the centre meets the chord at its midpoint.
2. Radius, distance and half chord make a right triangle with hypotenuse r.
3. Half chord² = r² − d², so half chord = √(r² − d²).
4. Chord = 2 × half chord = 2√(r² − d²).
Answer: The half chord is √(r² − d²) by Baudhāyana-Pythagoras, and the chord is twice it.

content.text:
★ Chord Length and Distance, Q3: In a circle, if the distance of chord AB from the centre is twice the distance of another chord CD from the centre, then can we conclude that CD = 2 AB? Give reasons for your answer.
1. Let CD be at distance d and AB at distance 2d.
2. CD = 2√(r² − d²) and AB = 2√(r² − 4d²).
3. Try r = 5, d = 1: CD = 2√24 ≈ 9.80 and AB = 2√21 ≈ 9.17.
4. 9.80 is nowhere near 2 × 9.17, so the lengths are not in ratio 2 : 1.
5. Only CD > AB follows (Theorem 8); the relation is not a simple doubling.
Answer: No. CD is longer than AB, but chord length does not change in proportion to distance.

video_script.design: One idea: the line from D through the centre makes two isosceles triangles whose outside angles at C are twice the angles at D. Assumes: base angles of an isosceles triangle, the exterior angle rule. Wrong idea: the slip says any point, even inside the circle, sees half. the answer to the closing question, 65°

maths_rules: Circle with centre C and radius 1 (scaled to the stage); positions in degrees anticlockwise from the rightward line through C
Cases: A at 220, B at 320, arc AFB through F at 270 (the lower arc), angle ACB = 100 degrees; D at 90 gives angle ADB = 50.0; D at 150 gives angle ADB = 50.0
Third case: A at 230, B at 310, angle ACB = 80 degrees; D at 90 gives angle ADB = 40.0
The slip's inside point P = (0, 0.5), halfway from C to the top of the circle, with A at 220 and B at 320: angle APB = 67.67, said as about 68 degrees; not 50
Proof, case 1 figure: A 220, B 320, D at 100, E at 280 (on arc AFB, since 280 lies between 220 and 320); D, C, E on one straight line
Case 1 check values (never spoken): angle CDB = angle CBD = 20, angle BCE = 40 = 2 x 20; angle CDA = angle CAD = 30, angle ACE = 60 = 2 x 30; angle BCA = 40 + 60 = 100 = 2 x 50 = 2 x angle BDA
CB = CD and CA = CD because all are radii; equal sides face equal angles, so angle CBD = angle CDB and angle CAD = angle CDA

Exterior angle rule: an outside angle of a triangle equals the two inside angles at the other corners added; angle BCE = angle CBD + angle CDB = 2 angle BDC; angle ACE = angle CAD + angle CDA = 2 angle CDA
Case 1: angle BCA = angle BCE + angle ECA, and angle BDA = angle BDC + angle CDA, so angle BCA = 2 angle BDA

Case 2 figure: A 220, B 320, D at 170, E at 350 (outside arc AFB); check values (never spoken): angle ADC = 65, angle ACE = 130; angle BDC = 15, angle BCE = 30; angle ACB = 130 - 30 = 100; angle ADB = 65 - 15 = 50
Case 2: angle ACB = angle ACE - angle BCE = 2 angle ADC - 2 angle BDC = 2 (angle ADC - angle BDC) = 2 angle ADB
The book's own letters: C is the centre, F marks the arc, E is where the line DC meets the circle again
Recap question: an arc makes 130 degrees at the centre; the angle at D on the rest of the circle is 130 / 2 = 65 degrees; never shown. The half-circle case is not asked here

media.description: A circle with a diameter, and a point D on it, gives the same reading wherever D sits. The video breaks the idea that any chord gives a right angle, states the corollary, derives it with a straight angle at the centre, and shows a second route through two isosceles triangles.

video_script.why: In every reading the angle at D stayed the same while AB passed through the centre; why is it always a right angle?

video_script.design: One idea: a diameter's arc sweeps a straight angle, and the angle at the circle is half of it, a right angle. Assumes: the angle at the centre is double the angle on the circle, and the angle sum of a triangle. Wrong idea: the slip carries the right angle over to any chord. The circle and the anchor question stay all video; two hard clears, before the proof and before the recap.

video_script.wrong_move: A common slip tilts the chord off the centre; points above now read 80 degrees and points below read 100 degrees, so the idea is struck through
maths_rules: Circle with centre C and radius 1 (scaled to the stage); positions in degrees anticlockwise from the rightward line through C
Diameter AB: A at 180, B at 0, so A, C, B lie on one straight line and angle ACB (the sweep along either half) is 180 degrees
Readings of angle ADB: D at 90 gives 90.0; D at 30 gives 90.0; D at 150 gives 90.0; D at 250 (below AB) gives 90.0

The slip's tilted chord: ends at 190 and 350, not through C; the lower arc between them sweeps 350 - 190 = 160 degrees at C; D at 90 (upper side) reads 80.0 = 160 / 2; D at 270 (lower side) reads 100.0 = (360 - 160) / 2; 80 + 100 = 180

Proof by the arc and angle theorem: take the arc from A to B not containing D; it sweeps from CA to CB a straight angle, 180 degrees; D is on the circle outside that arc, so angle ADB = 180 / 2 = 90 degrees

Second route: join D to C; CA = CD = CB (radii); in triangle DCA the base angles are equal, call each x; in triangle DCB the base angles are equal, call each y; triangle ADB has angles x at A, x + y at D, y at B; x + (x + y) + y = 180, so 2x + 2y = 180 and x + y = 90
Check of the second route with D at 30: x = angle CAD = 15, y = angle CBD = 75, x + y = 90 (never spoken)
A corollary is a fact that follows at once from a result already proved (the book's definition)
Recap question: if D sees a chord at a right angle, must the chord pass through the centre? Never answered here

media.tool_name: Standing on the rim, looking at a diameter
media.description: Standing on the rim, looking at a diameter. You drag a point D all the way round a circle while AB passes through the centre C, and watch the angle at D. You can join D to C, mark equal sides, write guesses, try to break them, and tilt AB off the centre. Starting scene: AB runs straight across through C and D sits just above A. Open question: AB passes through the centre. What angle does AB make at a point D on the circle, and does it depend on where D is? Patterns to look at, one per request, gentle to strong: (1) Look at the angle that AB makes at the centre C. (2) Join D to C and look at the two triangles DCA and DCB. (3) Mark the equal sides in each of those triangles, then look at the angles opposite them. (4) Look at the three angles of triangle ADB, split into pairs by CD. Break it: Switch off 'AB passes through the centre' and tilt AB off C: the angle at D moves away from its steady value, one way on the larger side and the other way on the smaller side. What stays fixed: The circle and its centre C stay fixed; D stays on the circle. The tutor: The tutor may ask whether the angle changes as D moves, suggest looking back at the previous tool, and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never states the angle, never gives a step, and never says right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time; your notebook and figure go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

content.text:
An arc of a circle is a connected portion of the circle. It is defined by two points on the circle, called the end points of the arc, and the curve connecting them along the circle's edge.
Look at the figure. A and B are two points on the circle. There are two ways of going from A to B. One goes via point X and one goes via point Y. The bigger of the two is called the major arc, and the smaller of the two is called the minor arc.
We define the angle subtended by the arc AB at the centre to be the measure of the angle AOB, as we sweep along the arc, so we move from OA to OB along the arc and measure the angle swept. The minor arc subtends the ∠AOB, here you move from OA to OB via X. The major arc subtends the angle we get as we move from OA to OB via Y.

content.text:
1. Two points A and B split the circle into two arcs.
2. The smaller is the minor arc, the bigger the major arc.
3. The angle an arc subtends at the centre is the angle swept from OA to OB along that arc.
4. The minor arc sweeps less than 180°, the major arc more than 180°; together they sweep 360°.

Arcs Check: A circle with centre O is drawn, and A, B, C, D are points on the circle (see the figure). Measure the angles subtended by arc AKB and arc CLD at the centre O. If the angle at the centre is less than 180°, it is a minor arc. If the angle at the centre is greater than 180°, it is a major arc. State whether arcs AKB and CLD are minor arcs or major arcs.
1. Sweep from OA to OB through K and measure: about 100°.
2. 100° < 180°, so arc AKB is a minor arc.
3. Sweep from OC to OD through L and measure: about 203°.
4. 203° > 180°, so arc CLD is a major arc.
Answer: Arc AKB is about 100°, a minor arc; arc CLD is about 203°, a major arc.

content.text:
By 'angle subtended by arc AXB at a point on the circle outside the arc' we mean the angle ACB where C is any point on the circle but not on arc AXB. Remarkably, the measure of this angle does not depend upon which specific point C we pick, so long as it is on the circle and outside the arc!
Activity: Draw a circle and a chord AB. Fix an arc AKB formed by AB and a point K between A, B on the circle. Measure the angle subtended at the centre by arc AKB. Take three points P, Q, R on the circle outside arc AKB. Measure the angles subtended by arc AKB at points P, Q, R. What do you notice?
Repeat this activity for a different arc AKB. Based on this activity, we can make a statement about the angles subtended by an arc of a circle at the centre and at a point of the circle outside the arc. We shall show that the following is true.

content.text:
Given: AFB is an arc. ∠ACB is the angle subtended by arc AFB at centre C. D is a point on the circle outside arc AFB. We will assume for now that D is such that DC when extended cuts the circle at some point E on arc AFB, as shown. We will consider the other case later. To show: ∠BCA = 2 ∠BDA.
Why is this true? Join D to C and extend DC to cut the circle at a point E on arc AFB. Now ∆DCB is isosceles with CB = CD. So, ∠CBD = ∠CDB. ∠BCE is the exterior angle of ∆BCD. By the exterior angle theorem, ∠BCE = ∠CBD + ∠CDB = 2 ∠BDC.
Similarly, ∆ADC is an isosceles triangle with CA = CD. So, ∠CAD = ∠CDA. ∠ACE is the exterior angle of ∆ADC. By the exterior angle theorem, ∠ACE = ∠CAD + ∠CDA = 2 ∠CDA. Now ∠BCA = ∠BCE + ∠ECA, and ∠BDA = ∠BDE + ∠EDA. Hence ∠BCA = 2 (∠BDC + ∠CDA) = 2 ∠BDA. So, ∠BCA = 2 ∠BDA.
The explanation we have given does not work if the situation is as shown in the second figure, where the extension of DC meets the circle at a point E outside the arc AFB. We must rework the explanation for this case.
Given: AFB is an arc. ∠ACB is the angle subtended by arc AFB at centre C. D is a point on the circle outside arc AFB such that when we extend DC it cuts the circle at some point E outside the arc AFB, as shown. We shall again make use of the properties of isosceles triangles.
∠ACE = ∠ADC + ∠CAD = 2 ∠ADC, since CA = CD (and so ∠ADC = ∠CAD). Similarly, ∠BCE = ∠BDC + ∠CBD = 2 ∠BDC. Also, ∠ACB = ∠ACE − ∠BCE, and ∠ADB = ∠ADC − ∠BDC. Hence ∠ACB = 2 ∠ADB.

We will assume for now that D is such that DC when extended cuts the circle at some point E on arc AFB, as shown. We will consider the other case later. To show: ∠BCA = 2 ∠BDA.

Why is this true? Join D to C and extend DC to cut the circle at a point E on arc AFB. Now ∆DCB is isosceles with CB = CD. So, ∠CBD = ∠CDB. ∠BCE is the exterior angle of ∆BCD. By the exterior angle theorem, ∠BCE = ∠CBD + ∠CDB = 2 ∠BDC.

Similarly, ∆ADC is an isosceles triangle with CA = CD. So, ∠CAD = ∠CDA. ∠ACE is the exterior angle of ∆ADC. By the exterior angle theorem, ∠ACE = ∠CAD + ∠CDA = 2 ∠CDA. Now ∠BCA = ∠BCE + ∠ECA, and ∠BDA = ∠BDE + ∠EDA. Hence ∠BCA = 2 (∠BDC + ∠CDA) = 2 ∠BDA. So, ∠BCA = 2 ∠BDA.

The explanation we have given does not work if the situation is as shown in the second figure, where the extension of DC meets the circle at a point E outside the arc AFB. We must rework the explanation for this case.

Given: AFB is an arc. ∠ACB is the angle subtended by arc AFB at centre C. D is a point on the circle outside arc AFB such that when we extend DC it cuts the circle at some point E outside the arc AFB, as shown. We shall again make use of the properties of isosceles triangles.
∠ACE = ∠ADC + ∠CAD = 2 ∠ADC, since CA = CD (and so ∠ADC = ∠CAD). Similarly, ∠BCE = ∠BDC + ∠CBD = 2 ∠BDC. Also, ∠ACB = ∠ACE − ∠BCE, and ∠ADB = ∠ADC − ∠BDC. Hence ∠ACB = 2 ∠ADB.

content.text:
Theorem 9: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of the circle is double the angle subtended by the arc at any point on the circle outside the arc.
Given: AFB is an arc, C is the centre, and D is a point on the circle outside arc AFB.
To show: ∠BCA = 2 ∠BDA.
1. Case 1: extend DC to meet the circle at E on arc AFB.
2. CB = CD, so ∠CBD = ∠CDB.
3. ∠BCE is an exterior angle of ∆BCD, so ∠BCE = ∠CBD + ∠CDB = 2 ∠BDC.
4. CA = CD, so ∠CAD = ∠CDA, and ∠ACE = ∠CAD + ∠CDA = 2 ∠CDA.
5. Add: ∠BCA = ∠BCE + ∠ECA = 2 (∠BDC + ∠CDA) = 2 ∠BDA.
6. Case 2: E lies outside arc AFB.
7. ∠ACE = 2 ∠ADC and ∠BCE = 2 ∠BDC, as before.
8. Subtract: ∠ACB = ∠ACE − ∠BCE = 2 (∠ADC − ∠BDC) = 2 ∠ADB.

content.text:
Something very interesting comes out of this. This is what the activity before Theorem 9 suggested. Take an arc AB. Decide how you want to go from A to B along the arc. Take any point D on the circle, outside arc AB.
Then, no matter where D is, so long as it is outside the arc and on the circle, ∠ADB is the same!
Let us understand this better using the figure. Consider the arc of the circle going from A to B via X. The points on the circle outside this arc are points you cross as you go from A to B via E. The angle subtended by AXB at the centre is the angle swept by CA as we move from CA to CB via X. Points E, F and D are all not on AXB. The theorem tells us that ∠AEB = ∠ADB = ∠AFB = 1/2 ∠ACB.
This fact that the angles in the same arc segment are all equal is a beautiful fact that distinguishes the circle from all other shapes.
In the figure, the angles that arc AB subtends at the points F, G outside the circle are different. For the points inside the circle, ∠AIB, ∠ACB and ∠AHB are all different. But for all points P on arc AB, the subtended angles are the same. Thus, for points D, E, ∠ADB = ∠AEB.

1. Each point D on the circle outside arc AXB gives ∠ADB = 1/2 ∠ACB.
2. The central angle does not depend on D, so neither does ∠ADB.
3. So ∠AEB = ∠ADB = ∠AFB: angles in the same segment are equal.
4. Points inside the circle see AB at a bigger angle, points outside at a smaller one: only the circle keeps it fixed.

content.text:
Corollary: The angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circle is 90°.
Corollary: A corollary is a fact that follows immediately from an already proved result.
Why is this true? Let AB be a diameter. We must show that ∠ADB is 90°. The arc from A to B we take is the arc not containing D. What is the angle subtended by that arc at C? We have to move from A along that arc till we reach B. So, the angle subtended is ∠ACB, a straight angle, 180°. Hence, ∠ADB = 1/2 ∠ACB = 90°.

the slip's point Y at 150 is nearer the chord than X at 60 is; it still reads 50 degrees
Part (ii): X at 60 above AB reads 50; Y at 250 below AB looks at the upper arc and reads 260 / 2 = 130 (computed 130.0); 50 + 130 = 180 because 100 + 260 = 360
Two angles that add to 180 are equal only when each is 90; each is 90 only when the arc sweeps 180, that is when AB is a diameter
Diameter case: A at 180, B at 0; X at 90 reads 90.0 and Y at 270 reads 90.0; X and Y are on opposite sides with equal angles, so the answer to (ii) is not always

content.text:
Angles in a Circle, Q1: In a circle with centre O, the central angle AOB is 60°. If the radius of the circle is 12 cm, what is the length of the chord AB?
1. OA = OB = 12 cm, so ΔOAB is isosceles with ∠O = 60°.
2. The base angles are (180° − 60°) ÷ 2 = 60° each.
3. So ΔOAB is equilateral and AB = OA.
Answer: AB = 12 cm.
steps: OA = OB = 12 cm, so ΔOAB is isosceles with ∠O = 60°.
The base angles are (180° − 60°) ÷ 2 = 60° each.
So ΔOAB is equilateral and AB = OA.

content.text:
Angles in a Circle, Q2: Let A and B be two points on a circle with centre O. (i) Are there points X, Y on the circle, on the same side of AB, such that ∠AXB is different from ∠AYB? (ii) Is it true that if ∠AXB = ∠AYB, then X and Y lie on the same side of the circle? (iii) If ∠AXB = ∠AYB, and X and Y do not lie on the circle, does the circle through A, B and X also pass through Y?
1. (i) Points on the same side of AB lie in the same segment, and each angle is half the same central angle.
2. (ii) On opposite sides the two angles add to 180°; they are equal only when both are 90°, that is, when AB is a diameter.
3. (iii) If X and Y are on the same side of AB, Theorem 10 puts A, B, X, Y on one circle.
4. If X and Y are on opposite sides of AB, the circle through A, B, X need not pass through Y.
Answer: (i) No. (ii) Not always: when AB is a diameter, X and Y can be on opposite sides with both angles 90°. (iii) Yes if X and Y are on the same side of AB; not necessarily otherwise.

Angles in a Circle, Q3: Find x in the figure.
1. ∠ADC = 100° stands on arc ABC, so that arc subtends 2 × 100° = 200° at the centre.
2. The other arc ADC subtends 360° − 200° = 160° at the centre.

media.description: Same view of AB from two places. You drag two points C and D on the same side of a segment AB and watch the angles ACB and ADB. You can keep the two angles equal while D moves, trace D, draw the circle through three points, write guesses, try to break them, and let D cross AB. Break it: Switch off 'C and D on the same side of AB' and let D cross over: it can keep the same angle yet leave the circle through A, B and C, apart from one special angle you may discover. What stays fixed: A and B stay fixed; the angle lock holds while you drag D. The tutor: The tutor may ask what the trail looks like, ask what happens just inside and just outside the circle, and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never states the result, never sets up the argument by contradiction for you, and never says right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time; your notebook, trail and figure go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

Given: C and D on the same side of AB, not on line AB, angle ACB = angle ADB. To prove: A, B, C, D lie on one circle
Construction: A, B, C are not on one line, so exactly one circle passes through them, because three points not on one line fix one circle

Case D inside, D = (0.6, 1.2): AD extended meets the circle at E = (1.086, 1.564); angle AEB = 50.0 = angle ACB; angle ADB is an outside angle of triangle BED at D, so angle ADB > angle AEB (71.6 > 50.0); with angle AEB = angle ACB = angle ADB this gives angle ADB > angle ADB, impossible

Outside angle rule used as an inequality: an outside angle of a triangle is bigger than each of the two inside angles at the other corners
The book writes 'exterior angle of BED' without the triangle sign; the video says triangle B E D

media.description: Four corners on one rim. You drag the four corners of a quadrilateral ABCD round a circle with centre O and build sums of any two of its angles. You can join corners to O, free C from the circle, draw the circle through three corners, write guesses, and try to break them. Starting scene: An uneven quadrilateral ABCD sits on the circle with O inside it. No sums are built. Open question: Four points on a circle make a quadrilateral. Is there a rule linking its angles? And if a quadrilateral follows that rule, must its corners lie on a circle? Patterns to look at, one per request, gentle to strong: (1) Look at the angle at A and the arc it faces, the arc through C from B to D. (2) Join O to B and O to D. Look at the two angles at O, the ordinary one and the reflex one. (3) Look at which angle at O belongs to the corner A and which belongs to the corner C. (4) For the reverse question, draw the circle through A, B and D, and look at where CD meets it; call that point E. Break it: Switch off 'C is on the circle' and drag C inside or outside: the sum of the opposite pair changes, one way inside and the other way outside. Let the corners cross over and the pairs that were opposite change too. What stays fixed: The circle and its centre O stay fixed; A, B and D stay on the circle. The tutor: The tutor may ask which pairs you have tried, ask what changes when C leaves the circle, and read out the next pattern when you ask. It never states the rule, never gives a step, and never says right or wrong. Hand over: Tap 'Take my ideas to the explanation' at any time; your sums, notebook and figure go with you, and the explanation follows whether or not you found a reason.

video_script.anchor: Do the opposite angles of a four-sided shape on a circle always add up to 180°?
video_script.design: One idea: the two opposite corners each take half of one of the two angles at the centre, and those two angles fill the whole turn. Assumes: the angle at the centre is double the angle at the rim, and a full turn of 360 degrees. Wrong idea: the slip says every four-sided shape does it; a rhombus off the circle breaks it. Transitions: the first picture gives way to a plain circle at the ground (one clear); the circle with ABCD stays from the ground through the idea; the diamond sits beside it in the break and leaves at the idea; the recap board replaces the proof board (second clear).
never_show: the answer to the closing question (no: two opposite angles both over 90° would add to more than 180°)
any claim that the rule holds for a four-sided shape whose corners are not on one circle
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip claims the rule holds for any four-sided shape; a rhombus with equal sides and angles 64, 116, 64, 116 has opposite angles adding to 128, and its fourth corner sits outside the circle through the other three
video_script.callback_to: the Four corners on one rim explore tool (M4.S7.T7.C32), where the student dragged four corners round a circle and summed pairs of angles
maths_rules: Every shape in the ground part is drawn on one circle with centre O; its corners A, B, C, D go round the rim in that order, and each corner angle is half of the arc (angle at O) it faces

The slip's rhombus: side 5 units, A = (0, 0), B = (5, 0), D = (5 cos 64°, 5 sin 64°), C = B + D. Angles A = 64°, B = 116°, C = 64°, D = 116°. Opposite A + C = 128°. The circle through A, B, D has radius about 2.95 units; C is about 5.53 units from its centre, so C is outside it

Proof, shape 1 values: A faces arc BCD, which makes reflex ∠BOD = 112 + 100 = 212°, and 212/2 = 106 = ∠A. C faces arc BAD, which makes the ordinary ∠BOD = 84 + 64 = 148°, and 148/2 = 74 = ∠C. 212 + 148 = 360

Proof: ∠BAD = 1/2 reflex ∠BOD and ∠BCD = 1/2 ∠BOD (the angle at the centre is double the angle at the rim, each corner outside the arc it faces); reflex ∠BOD + ∠BOD = 360°; so ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 1/2 × 360° = 180°
Other pair: the four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°, so ∠ABC + ∠CDA = 360° - 180° = 180°
Closing question, answer never shown: two opposite angles both greater than 90° would add to more than 180°, so no
video_script.payoff_line: Angle B eigh D plus angle B C D equals one hundred and eighty degrees

C pulled outside, along the radius to 1.3 times the radius: ∠BCD = 80.09°, read as 80°, and 83 + 80 = 163
C pushed inside, along the radius to 0.8 times the radius: ∠BCD = 111.43°, read as 111°, and 83 + 111 = 194
All readings computed from coordinates; readings to the nearest degree

The slip's trapezium: D = (0, 0), C = (8, 0), A = (-2.50, 4), B = (7.58, 4), AB parallel to DC. Angles A = 58°, B = 96°, C = 84°, D = 122°. A + D = 180 (side by side), opposite A + C = 58 + 84 = 142. The circle through A, B, D has radius about 5.05; C is about 6.99 from its centre, so C is outside it
Converse: the cyclic quadrilateral rule says corners on a circle give opposite angles adding to 180; this theorem turns it round
If ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180 then ∠ABC + ∠CDA = 360 - 180 = 180, since the four angles add to 360

Proof, C outside: A, B, D are not on one line, so exactly one circle passes through them (three points not on one line fix one circle). Segment CD meets the circle at E, between C and D. ABED is cyclic, so ∠BAD + ∠BED = 180 (cyclic quadrilateral rule). Given ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180, so ∠BED = ∠BCD. D, E, C lie on one line with E between, so ∠BED is the exterior angle of triangle BEC at E, and ∠BED = ∠EBC + ∠BCE > ∠BCE = ∠BCD. Contradiction
Figure values for the outside case (C at 1.3 times the radius): E is on the circle at about 210.9°. ∠BED = 97°, ∠BCD = 80.09° (read 80), ∠EBC = 16.91°; 80.09 + 16.91 = 97

C inside (the book leaves this case to the reader; the video proves it): stretch DC beyond C to meet the circle at E; ABED is cyclic, so ∠BED = ∠BCD as in the first case; D, C, E lie on one line with C between, so ∠BCD is the exterior angle of triangle BCE at C and ∠BCD = ∠CBE + ∠BEC > ∠BEC = ∠BED. Contradiction
Figure values for the inside case (C at 0.8 times the radius): E is on the circle at about 183.3°. ∠BED = ∠BEC = 97°, ∠BCD = 111.43° (read 111), ∠CBE = 14.43°; 97 + 14.43 = 111.43
Closing question: angles in order 112°, 79°, 68°, 101° (sum 360); opposite pairs 112 + 68 = 180 and 79 + 101 = 180, so yes, by this theorem; never shown

content.text:
As always we draw the picture first. Given: Consider segment AB. Points C and D lie on the same side of AB; points C and D are not on the line AB; and ∠ACB = ∠ADB. To show: A, B, C, D lie on the same circle.
Why is this true? The points A, B, C are noncollinear points. So, using Theorem 1, there is a circle passing through A, B, C. Let us show that D also lies on that circle. For this, let us draw the circle through A, B and C. Suppose D is not on the circle; then it is either inside or outside the circle. Join AD.
If D is outside the circle, then AD intersects the circle at E. If D is inside the circle, extend AD to meet the circle at E. Now C, E are on the same segment of the arc formed by chord AB. So, ∠ACB = ∠AEB.
If D were outside the circle, then ∠AEB is an exterior angle of the ∆BED, so ∠AEB > ∠ADB. Also, ∠AEB = ∠ACB (angles in the same segment of a circle), and ∠ACB = ∠ADB (given). This leads to ∠ACB being greater than itself, which is obviously not possible.
If D were inside the circle, then ∠ADB is an exterior angle of BED. In the same way that we argued above, we reach an impossible conclusion.
So, we must eliminate both of these options (D being outside the circle and D being inside the circle). So, D must be on the circle passing through A, B, C. In other words, A, B, C, D are concyclic.

content.text:
Theorem 10: If a line segment AB joining two points A, B subtends equal angles at two other points C, D that lie on the same side of AB, then the four points lie on a circle.
Given: C and D lie on the same side of AB, not on line AB, and ∠ACB = ∠ADB.
To show: A, B, C, D lie on the same circle.
1. A, B, C are not collinear, so by Theorem 1 a circle passes through them.
2. Suppose D is not on this circle; then D is outside it or inside it.
3. If D is outside, AD meets the circle at E.
4. C and E are in the same segment, so ∠AEB = ∠ACB.
5. ∠AEB is an exterior angle of ∆BED, so ∠AEB > ∠ADB = ∠ACB.
6. So ∠ACB > ∠ACB, which is impossible.
7. If D is inside, extend AD to meet the circle at E; now ∠ADB > ∠AEB = ∠ACB, again impossible.
8. So D lies on the circle, and A, B, C, D are concyclic.

content.text:
Given: A, B, C, D are the vertices of a cyclic 4-gon. This means that there is a circle passing through A, B, C, D. Let its centre be O. To show: ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180°.
How shall we show that this is true? Consider arc BCD; point A is on the circle and it lies outside the arc BCD. So ∠BAD is half the angle that arc BCD subtends at the centre O. Since we move from OB to OD along C, this is the reflex angle BOD (dotted). So, ∠BAD = 1/2 (reflex angle BOD).
Similarly, ∠BCD is half the angle subtended by the arc BAD at O. This is the angle denoted by the double arc BOD. Since C is on arc BCD, we need to move from OB to OD via A. So, ∠BCD = 1/2 (∠BOD).
So, ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 1/2 (complete angle at the centre O). A complete rotation at O is 360°. Hence, ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 1/2 × (360°) = 180°. So, the opposite angles of a cyclic 4-gon add up to 180°.
The converse of this theorem also holds.
