content.text:
Theorem 11: The sum of two opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180°.
Given: A, B, C, D are the vertices of a cyclic 4-gon, on a circle with centre O.
To show: ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180°.
1. A lies outside arc BCD, so ∠BAD = 1/2 (reflex ∠BOD).
2. C lies outside arc BAD, so ∠BCD = 1/2 (∠BOD).
3. The two angles at O make a complete turn.
4. So ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 1/2 × 360° = 180°.

content.text:
Given: ABCD is a 4-gon. ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180°. ∠ABC + ∠CDA = 180°. To show that: ABCD is cyclic.
Why is this true? Suppose ABCD is not cyclic. Since A, D, B are not collinear, there is a circle passing through the three points. If that circle does not pass through C, there are two cases: C is outside or C is inside the circle.
We deal only with the first case and leave the other to the reader. Let E be the point where CD meets the circle. Then ABED is a cyclic 4-gon. So from Theorem 11, ∠BAD + ∠BED = 180°. We are also given ∠BAD + ∠DCB = 180°.
So ∠BCD = ∠BED. But this is not possible as ∠BED is the exterior angle of BEC and hence greater than ∠BCE, i.e., greater than ∠BCD. So, points A, B, C, D all lie on a circle.

content.text:
Theorem 12: If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180°, then the vertices of the quadrilateral lie on a circle, i.e., they are concyclic.
Given: ABCD is a 4-gon with ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180°.
To show: ABCD is cyclic.
1. A, D, B are not collinear, so a circle passes through them.
2. Suppose C is outside this circle, and let CD meet the circle at E.
3. ABED is cyclic, so ∠BAD + ∠BED = 180° (Theorem 11).
4. Also ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180° (given), so ∠BCD = ∠BED.
5. But ∠BED is an exterior angle of ∆BEC, so ∠BED > ∠BCD.
6. This is impossible, so C lies on the circle and A, B, C, D are concyclic.

content.publication_text:
Theorem 12: If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180°, then the vertices of the quadrilateral lie on a circle, i.e., they are concyclic.
Given: ABCD is a 4-gon with ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180°.
To show: ABCD is cyclic.
1. A, D, B are not collinear, so a circle passes through them.
2. Suppose C is outside this circle, and let CD meet the circle at E.
3. ABED is cyclic, so ∠BAD + ∠BED = 180° (Theorem 11).
4. Also ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180° (given), so ∠BCD = ∠BED.
5. But ∠BED is an exterior angle of ∆BEC, so ∠BED > ∠BCD.
6. This is impossible, so C lies on the circle and A, B, C, D are concyclic.

content.text:
Cyclic Quadrilateral Check: A cyclic quadrilateral has angles measuring ∠A = 80°, ∠B = 110°, ∠C = 100°, and ∠D = 70°. Can such a quadrilateral be drawn? Explain why or why not.
1. Angle sum: 80° + 110° + 100° + 70° = 360°, as for any quadrilateral.
2. Opposite angles: ∠A + ∠C = 80° + 100° = 180°.
3. ∠B + ∠D = 110° + 70° = 180°.
4. By Theorem 12 a quadrilateral with these angles is cyclic.
Answer: Yes. Both pairs of opposite angles add to 180°, so it can be drawn in a circle.

video_script.design: One idea: the centre is the same distance from both ends of a chord, because both are radii. Assumes congruent triangles by three sides and angles on a straight line. maths_rules: a circle with centre O; A and B are two points on it; AB is a chord that does not pass through O (the diameter case is handled in the recap)
M is the midpoint of AB, so MA = MB
OA = OB because both are radii
triangles OMA and OMB: OA = OB, MA = MB, OM is shared, so they are congruent (side, side, side)
so angle OMA = angle OMB
angles OMA and OMB lie together on the straight line AB, so they add to 180°; equal, so each is 90°
OM passes through the midpoint M of AB at a right angle, so line OM is the perpendicular bisector of AB; there is only one such line
so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB (the book's route: O is the same distance from A and B, and every such point lies on the perpendicular bisector; the congruent triangles show why)
if AB is a diameter, M is O itself, and O lies on the perpendicular bisector at once
the fold that puts A onto B makes a crease through M at a right angle to AB, so the crease is the perpendicular bisector

video_script.design: One idea: equal distances from the centre make two congruent right triangles at the crossing. maths_rules: the circle is a circle, centre O = (0, 0), radius 5 m, drawn to scale
chord AB lies on y = 3 from A = (-4, 3) to B = (4, 3); 16 + 9 = 25, so A and B are on the circle; AB = 8 m
chord CD lies on x = 3 from C = (3, -4) to D = (3, 4); 9 + 16 = 25, so C and D are on the circle; CD = 8 m
they cross at P = (3, 3); OP = sqrt(9 + 9) = sqrt(18), about 4.24 m, less than 5, so P is inside the circle
M = (0, 3) is the foot of the perpendicular from O to AB and N = (3, 0) the foot from O to CD; OM = ON = 3 m
angle OMP = angle ONP = 90 degrees; OP is common; OM = ON; so triangle OMP is congruent to triangle ONP (right angle, hypotenuse, side); MP = NP = 3 m
M is the midpoint of AB and N the midpoint of CD (the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord); AM = CN = 4 m
the ends are named so that A and C are the ends farther from P: AP = AM + MP = 4 + 3 = 7 m and CP = CN + NP = 4 + 3 = 7 m
PB = AB - AP = 8 - 7 = 1 m and PD = CD - CP = 8 - 7 = 1 m
if P is the midpoint of one chord then MP = 0, so NP = 0 and all four pieces are 4 m; this is a special case, not the rule
the slip's claim of four equal pieces fails in the drawn circle: 7 m and 1 m

a parallelogram with a right angle is a rectangle

M = midpoint of AB = (-2, 1); N = midpoint of AC = (2, 1)
OM ⊥ AB: (-2, 1) · (-4, -8) = 8 - 8 = 0; ON ⊥ AC in the same way
OM = ON = √5, about 2.24 units: equal chords are at the same distance from the centre (the chapter's result on equal chords)
in triangles OMA and ONA: ∠OMA = ∠ONA = 90°, OA is shared and is the side opposite the right angle, OM = ON
right angle, side opposite it, one side (RHS): ΔOMA ≅ ΔONA, so ∠OAM = ∠OAN
M lies on AB and N lies on AC, so ∠OAM = ∠OAB and ∠OAN = ∠OAC; hence ∠OAB = ∠OAC and AO halves ∠BAC
the slip's case: C moves to C2 = (5, 0) so AC2 = √50, about 7.07, not equal to AB; the line halving ∠BAC2 passes about 0.80 units from O, drawn to scale so the miss is visible
check route: triangles OAB and OAC have OA shared, OB = OC = 5 (radii), AB = AC, so ΔOAB ≅ ΔOAC (SSS) and ∠OAB = ∠OAC again

video_script.anchor: A regular hexagon sits in a circle of radius r. How long is each side, and how far is each side from the centre?
video_script.design: One idea: six equal angles at the centre make six triangles with all sides r, and half a side gives a right triangle for the distance. Assumes equal chords make equal angles at the centre, the perpendicular from the centre halves a chord, and Baudhayana-Pythagoras. Wrong idea: The slip measures to a corner. maths_rules: the circle has centre O and radius r; on screen r is drawn as 5 units, labelled r, never as a number
the six corners sit on the rim at 0°, 60°, 120°, 180°, 240° and 300° from O
the six sides are equal chords, so the six angles at the centre are equal: 360° ÷ 6 = 60° each
each triangle has two sides r (radii), so its base angles are equal: (180° - 60°) ÷ 2 = 60° each
all three angles are 60°, so the triangle has all three sides equal: each side of the hexagon = r
the line from O at right angles to a side meets it at its midpoint (the perpendicular from the centre halves a chord), so half the side = r/2
right triangle with hypotenuse r and one leg r/2: d² = r² - (r/2)² = r² - r²/4 = 3r²/4
check with r = 10 cm: side 10 cm, d = 8.66 cm, about 8.7 cm
the slip's r is the distance from O to a corner, not to the side; it is struck
video_script.payoff_line: Each side is r, and its distance from the centre is root three over two, times r

final_answer.spoken: each side is r, and its distance from the centre is root three over two, times r

video_script.wrong_answer: the distance to a side is r
video_script.fraction_reading: root three over two; three quarters; half of r

Watch for this slip: measuring the distance to a corner, which gives r, instead of straight to the middle of the side.

video_script.anchor: MNOP on a circle, MN a diameter. What can you say about ∠MOP and ∠MNP?
video_script.design: One idea: two angles on the same chord, from the same side, are equal; the diameter adds two right angles. Assumes angles in the same segment and the angle in a semicircle. Wrong idea: The slip reads O as the centre. The anchor and the circle figure stay all video; one clear of the working band before the recap.

maths_rules: O is a vertex of the quadrilateral, not the centre; the centre is the midpoint of MN and is drawn as an unlabelled dot
drawn: circle radius 5 centred at (0, 0); M = (−5, 0), N = (5, 0), O = (2.5, −4.33), P = (−2.5, −4.33); going round, M, N, O, P
N and O lie on the same side of the chord MP, so ∠MOP and ∠MNP are angles in the same segment and are equal
in the drawing: ∠MNP = 30° and ∠MOP = 30° (each is half of the 60° arc MP)
MN is a diameter, so ∠MON = 90° and ∠MPN = 90° (angle in a semicircle)
the slip's rule (angle at the centre is double) needs the vertex at the centre; O is on the circle, so it does not apply
video_script.payoff_line: That means angle M O P equals angle M N P

final_answer.spoken: angle M O P equals angle M N P, and angles M O N and M P N are both ninety degrees

video_script.substitution: Both angles open onto the chord M P from the same side, so they are equal.

video_script.anchor: ABCD on a circle, AD stretched past D to E. Why is ∠CDE = ∠ABC?
video_script.design: One idea: two different angles that each make 180 with the same angle are equal. Assumes angles on a line and the cyclic quadrilateral angle fact. Wrong idea: The slip pairs the outside angle with its neighbour. The anchor and the circle figure stay all video; one clear of the working band before the recap.
never_show: ∠CDE = ∠ADC marked as right
video_script.wrong_move: The slip pairs the outside angle with the angle beside it at D; the drawing measures ∠ADC = 115° and ∠CDE = 65°, so the pairing is struck
maths_rules: E is on side AD stretched past D, so A, D, E lie on one straight line and ∠CDE is the outside angle at D
∠CDE + ∠ADC = 180° (angles side by side on a straight line)
∠ABC + ∠ADC = 180° (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral)
both equal 180° − ∠ADC, so ∠CDE = ∠ABC
drawn: circle radius 5 centred at (0, 0); A = (−4.70, −1.71), B = (0.87, 4.92), C = (4.33, −2.50), D = (0, −5), E = (3.76, −7.63) on AD stretched past D
in the drawing: ∠ADC = 115°, ∠ABC = 65°, ∠CDE = 65°; 115 + 65 = 180
the slip's pairing ∠CDE = ∠ADC holds only when both are 90°
video_script.payoff_line: The same amount is left, so angle C D E equals angle eigh B C

final_answer.spoken: angle C D E equals angle eigh B C

video_script.substitution: Angle C D E and angle eigh B C both make one hundred and eighty with angle eigh D C.
video_script.wrong_answer: angle C D E equals angle eigh D C
open_questions: The book says E is on the extension of side CD, but then C, D, E are on one line and angle CDE is a straight angle. For angle CDE to be the outside angle at D, E must be on side AD stretched past D; the video uses that reading. Suggest adding this to SOLUTION_NOTES.

video_script.anchor: Why is no chord of a circle longer than its diameter?
video_script.design: One idea: two radii make the diameter, and a straight side is shorter than the path through O. Assumes the triangle rule (one side is shorter than the other two together). Wrong idea: The slip treats a few measurements as a proof. The circle and the anchor stay all video; one clear of the slip's chords before the idea part, and one clear of the working band before the recap.

maths_rules: the figure is a circle with centre O and radius r; on screen r is drawn as 5 units, so the diameter is 10 units
the sample chord AB has A = (-3, 4) and B = (5, 0): both are 5 from O; AB = √(8² + 4²) = √80, about 8.94 units, shorter than 10
OA = OB = r because A and B are on the circle; OA + OB = 2r, the diameter
in triangle OAB, AB < OA + OB (one side of a triangle is shorter than the other two added together)
so AB < 2r when AB misses O
when AB passes through O there is no triangle: A, O and B are on one line and AB = OA + OB = 2r, a diameter
together: AB ≤ 2r for every chord, with AB = 2r only for a diameter
the slip's five chords are drawn at distances 4, 3, 2, 1.5 and 1 units from O, lengths 2√(25 - d²): 6, 8, about 9.17, about 9.54, about 9.80 units, each shorter than 10
check: a chord at distance d from O has length 2√(r² - d²); with r = 5, d = 4 gives 6, d = 3 gives 8, d = 0 gives 10, the longest

video_script.anchor: A is a point inside a circle with centre O. Why is the chord through A at right angles to OA the shortest one through A?
video_script.design: One idea: a chord through A is never farther than OA from O, and farther means shorter. Assumes the perpendicular from the centre halves a chord, and Baudhayana-Pythagoras. Wrong idea: The slip picks the chord through the centre. The circle, O, A and the anchor stay all video; one clear of the slip's chord before the idea part, and one clear of the working band before the recap.
never_show: the diameter through A marked as the shortest
video_script.wrong_move: The slip lays the chord along the line from O through A, thinking the path through the centre is the most direct. The picture shows this chord is the diameter, and the ruler shows it is the longest one through A, so the choice is struck.
maths_rules: the figure is a circle with centre O = (0, 0) and radius 5 units; the point is A = (3, 0), so OA = 3; A is not the centre
the chord at right angles to OA is the line x = 3: its ends are (3, 4) and (3, -4), since 3² + 4² = 25; its length is 8 units and its distance from O is 3 = OA
a slanted chord through A at 45° to OA: distance from O is OM = 3 × sin 45° = 3/√2, about 2.12; OM² = 4.5; length = 2√(25 - 4.5) = 2√20.5, about 9.06 units
the chord along OA is the diameter: distance 0, length 10 units
for any chord through A, drop OM at right angles to it; triangle OMA has its right angle at M, so OA is the side opposite the right angle and OM ≤ OA
OM = OA only when M is at A, that is, when the chord is at right angles to OA

the line from O at right angles to a chord halves it, so (half chord)² = r² - OM² (Baudhayana-Pythagoras): a larger OM gives a shorter chord (the chapter's result that the longer chord is nearer the centre, read the other way)
so the chord at right angles to OA, with the largest possible distance OA, is the shortest: 8 < 9.06 < 10 in the drawing
if A were the centre O, every chord through A would be a diameter and all would be equal; the question takes A inside the circle and different from O
video_script.payoff_line: The chord at right angles to O eigh is the shortest chord through eigh

final_answer.value: every chord through A is at most OA from O; the chord ⊥ OA is exactly OA away, so it is the shortest
final_answer.spoken: the chord at right angles to O eigh is the farthest from the centre, so it is the shortest

video_script.substitution: A chord through A is never farther than OA from the centre, and the farther a chord is from the centre, the shorter it is.

video_script.anchor: ABCD has all four corners on a circle with centre O. How does the figure show that opposite angles add to 180°?
video_script.design: One idea: equal radii make each corner two base angles, and every letter is used twice round the shape. Assumes the angles of a quadrilateral add to 360 degrees and equal sides give equal base angles. Wrong idea: The slip drops the circle. The circle, ABCD and the anchor stay all video; one clear of the slip's parallelogram before the idea part, and one clear of the working band before the recap.
never_show: 180° as the sum of opposite angles of the parallelogram
video_script.wrong_move: The slip says opposite angles of any four-sided shape add to 180 degrees. A parallelogram with angles 60 and 120 degrees is drawn off the circle; its opposite angles 60 and 60 add to 120, so the idea is struck.
maths_rules: the figure is a circle with centre O and radius 5 units; the corners follow the book's layout: A at 110°, B at 220°, C at 350° and D at 70° measured round O, so A is upper left, B lower left, C lower right and D right
OA = OB = OC = OD = 5 (radii), so triangles OAB, OBC, OCD and ODA each have two equal sides and equal base angles
as in the book's figure: p = ∠OAB, q = ∠OBC, u = ∠OCD, v = ∠ODA; by equal base angles ∠OBA = p, ∠OCB = q, ∠ODC = u, ∠OAD = v
the angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°: (p + v) + (p + q) + (q + u) + (u + v) = 2(p + q + u + v) = 360°, so p + q + u + v = 180°
∠A + ∠C = (p + v) + (q + u) = 180°; in the drawing 105 + 75 = 180; likewise ∠B + ∠D = 60 + 120 = 180
O lies inside ABCD in this figure (every angle at O is under 180°), which is the case the book's figure shows
the slip's shape: a parallelogram with angles 60°, 120°, 60°, 120°, not on a circle; opposite angles 60 + 60 = 120, not 180
video_script.payoff_line: Angle eigh plus angle C is one hundred and eighty degrees

final_answer.spoken: angle eigh plus angle C uses each letter once, so it is one hundred and eighty degrees

video_script.substitution: Each corner is two base angles, every letter is used at two corners, so all four corners make twice p + q + u + v, and one pair of opposite corners uses each letter once.
video_script.wrong_answer: any four-sided shape

Chapter Exercises, Q5: Prove that the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre of the circle.
1. Let AB be a chord of a circle with centre O.
2. OA = OB (radii), so O is equidistant from A and B.
3. Every point equidistant from A and B lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
4. So O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
Answer: The centre is equidistant from the ends of the chord, so it lies on the chord's perpendicular bisector.

Chapter Exercises, Q8: Quadrilateral PQRS is inscribed in a circle. If ∠P = (2x + 10)° and ∠R = (3x − 20)°, find the value of x and the measures of ∠P and ∠R.
1. ∠P and ∠R are opposite, so (2x + 10) + (3x − 20) = 180.
2. 5x − 10 = 180, so 5x = 190 and x = 38.
3. ∠P = 2 × 38 + 10 = 86°.
4. ∠R = 3 × 38 − 20 = 94°.
5. Check: 86° + 94° = 180°.
Answer: x = 38, ∠P = 86° and ∠R = 94°.

Chapter Exercises, Q10: A cyclic quadrilateral has sides 5, 5, 12, 12 units. Find its area.
1. Say AB = AD = 5 and CB = CD = 12; ΔABC ≅ ΔADC by SSS, so ∠B = ∠D.
2. ∠B + ∠D = 180° (Theorem 11), so ∠B = ∠D = 90°.
3. Area = 2 × (1/2 × 5 × 12) = 60 square units.
4. If the sides alternate 5, 12, 5, 12, the quadrilateral is a 5 by 12 rectangle: area 5 × 12 = 60.
Answer: 60 square units, whichever order the sides come in.

★ Chapter Exercises, Q11: Consider a cyclic quadrilateral. Without drawing its circumcircle, how can we find out whether the centre of the circumcircle lies inside the quadrilateral or outside? What is the best way of finding out?
1. By Theorem 9, the centre is on the same side of a side AB as the other two vertices exactly when AB subtends an acute angle at them.
2. So look at each side and the angle it makes at a vertex not on it, for example ∠ACB for side AB.
3. If all four such angles are acute, the centre is inside.
4. If one is obtuse, the centre is outside, beyond that side; if one is 90°, the centre lies on that side.
Answer: Check the angle each side subtends at an opposite vertex: all acute means the centre is inside; one obtuse means it is outside.

★ Chapter Exercises, Q12: When two chords intersect, each of them is divided into two line segments. Show that if the intersecting chords are of equal length, then the line segments of one chord are equal to the corresponding line segments of the other chord.
1. Let equal chords AB and CD meet at P; drop OM ⊥ AB and ON ⊥ CD.
2. Equal chords are equidistant from the centre (Theorem 6), so OM = ON.
3. OP is common and ∠OMP = ∠ONP = 90°, so ΔOMP ≅ ΔONP (RHS) and MP = NP.
4. M and N are midpoints (Theorem 5), so AM = CN.
5. AP = AM + MP = CN + NP = CP, and PB = AB − AP = CD − CP = PD.
Answer: AP = CP and PB = PD.

★ Chapter Exercises, Q14: Show that rectangle is the only parallelogram that can be inscribed in a circle.
1. In a parallelogram ABCD, opposite angles are equal: ∠A = ∠C.
2. If it is inscribed in a circle, ∠A + ∠C = 180° (Theorem 11).
3. So ∠A = ∠C = 90°, and a parallelogram with a right angle is a rectangle.
Answer: A cyclic parallelogram has all angles 90°, so it is a rectangle.

★ Chapter Exercises, Q16: Consider all chords of a circle of a fixed length. What is the shape formed by the midpoints of all these chords?
1. Chords of the same length are all at the same distance d from the centre (Theorem 6).
2. The line from the centre to a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to it, so each midpoint is exactly d from the centre.
3. d = √(r² − (half the length)²) is the same for every such chord.
Answer: A circle with the same centre and radius √(r² − (l/2)²), where l is the fixed length.

★ Chapter Exercises, Q17: In a circle with centre O, chords AB and AC are congruent. Explain why this statement is true: "The centre of the circle lies on the angle bisector of ∠BAC".
1. AB = AC, so the chords are equidistant from O: OM = ON, with OM ⊥ AB and ON ⊥ AC.
2. OA is common and ∠OMA = ∠ONA = 90°.
3. By RHS, ΔOMA ≅ ΔONA, so ∠OAM = ∠OAN.
4. So AO bisects ∠BAC, and O lies on the bisector.
Answer: O is equidistant from the two equal chords, so AO makes equal angles with them.

Chapter Exercises, Q18: Two parallel chords of lengths 10 cm and 24 cm are on the same side of the centre of a circle. The distance between the chords is 7 cm. Find the radius of the circle.
1. Half chords are 5 cm and 12 cm; let the 24 cm chord be x cm from the centre.
2. The 10 cm chord is shorter, so it is farther: x + 7 cm from the centre.
3. r² = 12² + x² = 5² + (x + 7)².
4. 144 + x² = 25 + x² + 14x + 49, so 14x = 70 and x = 5.
5. r² = 144 + 25 = 169, so r = 13 cm.
Answer: 13 cm.
steps: Half chords are 5 cm and 12 cm; let the 24 cm chord be x cm from the centre.
The 10 cm chord is shorter, so it is farther: x + 7 cm from the centre.
r² = 12² + x² = 5² + (x + 7)².

★ Chapter Exercises, Q19: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius r. Find the length of the sides of the hexagon and the distance of each side from the centre of the circle.
1. Each side subtends 360° ÷ 6 = 60° at the centre.
2. The triangle formed by a side and two radii is equilateral, so each side is r.
3. Distance = √(r² − (r/2)²) = √(3r²/4) = (√3/2) r.
Answer: Each side is r, and each side is (√3/2) r, about 0.87 r, from the centre.

Chapter Exercises, Q20: A quadrilateral MNOP is inscribed in a circle. If MN is a diameter, what can you say about ∠MOP and ∠MNP? Explain your reasoning.
1. Here O is a vertex of the quadrilateral, not the centre.
2. Going round the circle M, N, O, P, the points N and O lie on the same side of the chord MP.
3. So ∠MOP and ∠MNP are angles in the same segment on chord MP, and they are equal.
4. Also MN is a diameter, so ∠MON = ∠MPN = 90° (angle in a semicircle).
Answer: ∠MOP = ∠MNP (angles in the same segment); and since MN is a diameter, ∠MON = ∠MPN = 90°.

Chapter Exercises, Q21: Let ABCD be a cyclic quadrilateral. Explain why the exterior angle at any vertex is equal to the interior opposite angle (e.g., ∠CDE = ∠ABC, where E is a point on the extension of side CD).
1. ∠CDE + ∠ADC = 180° (angles on a line).
2. ∠ABC + ∠ADC = 180° (Theorem 11).
3. So ∠CDE = ∠ABC.
Answer: Both ∠CDE and ∠ABC make 180° with ∠ADC, so they are equal.
steps: ∠CDE + ∠ADC = 180° (angles on a line).

So ∠CDE = ∠ABC.

★ Chapter Exercises, Q22: "There is no chord of a circle that is longer than its diameter." How do you justify this statement?
1. Let AB be any chord of a circle with centre O and radius r.
2. In ΔOAB (or on a line, if AB passes through O), AB ≤ OA + OB.
3. OA + OB = 2r, which is the diameter.
4. Equality holds only when O lies on AB, that is, when AB is a diameter.
Answer: By the triangle inequality AB ≤ OA + OB = 2r, the diameter.

★ Chapter Exercises, Q23: Let A be any point within a given circle with centre O. Show that the shortest chord of the circle that passes through point A is the one that is perpendicular to OA.
1. For a chord through A, let M be the foot of the perpendicular from O; then OM ≤ OA (OA is a hypotenuse).
2. OM = OA exactly when the chord is perpendicular to OA at A.
3. By Theorem 8 the chord farther from the centre is the shorter one.
4. So the chord perpendicular to OA, which is the farthest possible, is the shortest.
Answer: Every chord through A is at distance at most OA from O, and the chord perpendicular to OA reaches that distance, so it is the shortest.

Chapter Exercises, Q24: How would you use the following figure to justify the statement that the angle in a semicircle is 90°?
1. OA equals each half of the diameter, so both triangles with vertex A and apex O are isosceles.
2. So the angles at A are a and b, and ∠A = a + b.
3. Angle sum of the big triangle: a + b + (a + b) = 180°.
4. So a + b = 90°, and the angle at A is a right angle.
Answer: The two isosceles triangles give ∠A = a + b and 2(a + b) = 180°, so ∠A = 90°.

★ Chapter Exercises, Q25: In a circle, two chords CC' and DD' are drawn perpendicular to a diameter AB. Prove that the segment MM' joining the midpoints of the chords CD and C'D' is perpendicular to AB.
1. AB is perpendicular to CC' and passes through the centre, so it bisects CC' (Theorem 5); likewise DD'.
2. So C' is the mirror image of C in AB, and D' is the mirror image of D.
3. Reflection in AB takes segment CD to segment C'D', so it takes M to M'.
4. A point and its mirror image are joined by a segment perpendicular to the mirror, so MM' ⊥ AB.
Answer: M' is the reflection of M in AB, so MM' is perpendicular to AB.

★ Chapter Exercises, Q26: How would you use the following figure to justify the statement that the sum of the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180°?
1. OA = OB = OC = OD (radii), so the four triangles at O are isosceles.
2. Their base angles pair up: ∠A = p + v, ∠B = p + q, ∠C = q + u, ∠D = u + v.
3. Angles of the quadrilateral: 2(p + q + u + v) = 360°, so p + q + u + v = 180°.
4. ∠A + ∠C = p + v + q + u = 180°.
Answer: Split the quadrilateral into four isosceles triangles at O; the base angles show ∠A + ∠C = 180°.

Their base angles pair up: ∠A = p + v, ∠B = p + q, ∠C = q + u, ∠D = u + v.

Board lines: 1 circle as all points at one distance from the centre, all radii equal; 2 exactly one circle through three points not on one line; 3 equal chords make equal angles at the centre, and the other way round; 4 the line from the centre to a chord's midpoint is at right angles to it, and the other way round; 5 equal chords are the same distance from the centre, and the other way round; 6 the longer chord is nearer the centre; 7 the angle at the centre is double the angle at the rim, and a diameter makes a right angle at the rim ; 8 equal angles on one side of a segment put four points on one circle; 9 opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180 degrees, and the other way round

First question settled: folding the paper circle so two rim points meet makes a crease that cuts that chord in half at right angles, and that crease passes through the centre; two such creases cross at the centre
Second question settled: four points lie on one circle when two opposite angles of the quadrilateral add to 180 degrees, or when a segment makes equal angles at the other two points on one side

Closing question: four dots joined in order give angles 94, 121, 86, 59 degrees; total 94 + 121 + 86 + 59 = 360; opposite pairs 94 + 86 = 180 and 121 + 59 = 180, so yes, by the converse of the cyclic quadrilateral rule; the answer is never shown
No number of any book question is used

content.text:
- A circle is the set of all points in a plane that lie at a given distance (the radius) from a fixed point called its centre.
- A circle has reflection symmetry across any diameter.
- A circle has rotational symmetry about its centre, through any angle.
- Infinitely many circles can be drawn through two given points. The centres of these circles lie on the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining the two given points.
- Given any three points not on a straight line, a unique circle can be drawn through them; it is called the circumcircle of the triangle whose vertices are the three given points. The centre of this circle is called the circumcentre of the three points, lies at the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the line segments joining the points.
- Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre of the circle. Conversely, if two chords subtend equal angles at the centre, the chords are equal in length.
- A line drawn from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to that chord. Conversely, a perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it.
- Chords of equal length lie at equal distance from the centre. Conversely, chords that lie at the same distance from the centre are equal in length.
- Given two unequal chords, the longer chord is closer to the centre.
- The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of a circle is twice the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle.
- The angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circle is 90°.
- If a line segment between two points subtends equal angles at two other points on the same side of the segment, all four points lie on a single circle (i.e., the points are concyclic).
- A quadrilateral inscribed in a circle is called cyclic. In a cyclic quadrilateral, the sum of opposite pairs of angles is 180°. Conversely, if two opposite angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180°, then it is a cyclic quadrilateral.

content.text: The circle is a beautiful and tantalising shape. After mastering these basic properties, you will get a feel for the symmetries of a circle and the properties of chords, the angles they subtend, the distances of chords from the centre, and angles subtended by arcs at the centre. Next year you will study many more interesting and beautiful such results about circles. Stay tuned, the best is yet to come!

objectives.objective_text: State the locus definition of a circle and mark the centre, a radius, a chord, its angle at the centre and a diameter on a given figure.
Explain why a turned circle looks unchanged at any angle, and show by folding that each crease through the centre is a diameter and a line of reflection symmetry.
Label chord, radius, diameter and arc on unfamiliar circle figures, including a long chord that misses the centre, and justify each label by the property it satisfies.
Show that every point of the perpendicular bisector of AB is the centre of a circle through A and B, and identify the smallest such circle.
State Theorem 1, that exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points, then test it by locating the centre with perpendicular bisectors and explain why collinear points have no circle.
Explain why Theorem 1 holds: the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC meet at exactly one centre; then locate the circumcentre of acute, obtuse and right triangles.
Construct circumcircles for given triangles, decide whether each centre lies inside or outside, find the least radius through two points, and explain why collinear points share no circle.
State Theorem 2, that equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre, and test it by turning and moving chords of equal length.
Prove Theorem 2, that equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre, using SSS congruence with two pairs of radii and the given equal chords.
Prove Theorem 3, that chords subtending equal angles at the centre are equal, using SAS congruence after explaining the arm-stretching picture.
State Theorem 4, that the line joining the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord, and test it on chords of every length.
Prove Theorem 4, that the line from the centre to a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to the chord, using SAS congruence and angles on a line.
Show that a chord and the centre form an isosceles triangle, and prove two such triangles on equal bases congruent.
Prove Theorem 5, that a perpendicular dropped from the centre to a chord bisects it, then use it for an inscribed isosceles triangle and two parallel chords.
State Theorem 6, that chords of equal length are equidistant from the centre, and test it by folding, tracing and moving equal chords.
Prove Theorem 6, that chords of equal length are equidistant from the centre, in two ways: SSS with equal altitudes, and RHS on the half chords.
State Theorem 8, that of two unequal chords the longer one is nearer the centre, and test it by recording chord lengths against their distances.
Prove Theorem 8, that the longer of two chords is nearer the centre, using Baudhāyana-Pythagoras, and explain why the diameter is the longest chord.
Prove Theorem 7, that chords equidistant from the centre are equal, by RHS and by Baudhāyana-Pythagoras, and prove Theorem 6 again with Baudhāyana-Pythagoras.
Compute a chord from the radius and distance, justify the formula 2√(r² − d²), and decide whether doubling a distance halves a chord.
Name the minor and major arcs on two points, measure the angle each sweeps at the centre, and classify the arcs AKB and CLD in the given figure.
State Theorem 9, that the angle an arc subtends at the centre is twice the angle it subtends at any point on the rest of the circle, and test it.
Prove Theorem 9, that an arc's angle at the centre is twice its angle at any point on the rest of the circle, in both cases, and order the proof's lines.
Explain why every point on the circle outside an arc sees it at the same angle, and contrast points inside and outside the circle where the angle changes.
State the corollary that a diameter subtends 90° at every point of the circle, test it, and derive it from Theorem 9 with a central angle of 180°.
Compute a chord from its central angle, decide when two angles on the same chord agree, and find an unknown angle in an inscribed quadrilateral.
State Theorem 10, that if segment AB subtends equal angles at C and D on the same side of AB, then A, B, C and D are concyclic, and test it.
Prove Theorem 10 by contradiction: a point that sees AB at the same angle as C cannot lie inside or outside the circle through A, B and C.
Define a cyclic quadrilateral and state Theorem 11, that each pair of its opposite angles adds to 180°, then test it by moving a vertex on and off the circle.
Prove Theorem 11, that each pair of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral adds to 180°, using Theorem 9, and decide whether given angles can form one.
Prove Theorem 12, the converse: a quadrilateral whose opposite angles add to 180° is cyclic, by contradiction using the exterior angle of a triangle.
Compute chord lengths, distances, radii and angles in circles, and justify angle facts about diameters and cyclic quadrilaterals, naming the theorem each step uses.
Write proofs and constructions that combine several theorems, such as equal intersecting chords, cyclic parallelograms, loci of midpoints and shortest chords.
Restate the chapter's definitions and twelve theorems in pairs of statement and converse, and settle both predictions made at the start of the chapter.

source_metadata.design: new_design (docs/25 playbook) with the Class 9 prompt's overrides: introduction topic first; one topic per big idea in the order definitions and symmetries, how many circles, chords and their angles with midpoints and perpendicular bisectors, distance from the centre, angles subtended by an arc, concyclicity; each theorem statement opens a tool so the student tries to prove it, then the book's proof with an explanatory video; every exercise question has its own video and a question-only image; Think and Reflect is enrichment; end-of-chapter exercises in their own topic (core and starred apart) before the summary.

Th1.name: Theorem 1
Th1.statement: There is a unique circle passing through three non-collinear points.

Th2.name: Theorem 2
Th2.statement: Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre of the circle.

Th3.name: Theorem 3
Th3.statement: Chords of a circle that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal.

Th4.name: Theorem 4
Th4.statement: The line joining the centre of a circle and the midpoint of a chord of the circle is perpendicular to the chord.

Th5.name: Theorem 5
Th5.statement: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord of the circle bisects the chord.

Th6.name: Theorem 6
Th6.statement: Chords of a circle having the same length are all at the same distance from the centre of the circle.

Th7.name: Theorem 7
Th7.statement: Chords of a circle that are equidistant from the centre have equal length.

Th8.name: Theorem 8
Th8.statement: Let AB and DE be two chords of a circle with centre C. Suppose AB > DE. Then the distance from C to AB is less than the distance from C to DE.

Th9.name: Theorem 9
Th9.statement: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of the circle is double the angle subtended by the arc at any point on the circle outside the arc.

Cor1.name: Corollary
Cor1.statement: The angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circle is 90°.

Th10.name: Theorem 10
Th10.statement: If a line segment AB joining two points A, B subtends equal angles at two other points C, D that lie on the same side of AB, then the four points lie on a circle.

Th11.name: Theorem 11
Th11.statement: The sum of two opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180°.

Th12.name: Theorem 12
Th12.statement: If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180°, then the vertices of the quadrilateral lie on a circle, i.e., they are concyclic.

source_metadata.chapter_idea: One sentence, 'every point of a circle is the same distance from its centre', is turned into a definition and then into twelve theorems: how many circles pass through given points, what the centre knows about every chord, how far each chord sits from the centre, what angle an arc makes at the centre and on the circle, and when four points share one circle.
